children.title: Positive Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where relaxed optimal values differ from Monge optimal values.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation between deterministic and relaxed transport values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \[C_M:=\inf_{T_\#\mu=
u}\int_X c(x,T(x))\,d\mu(x),\qquad C_K:=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,
u)}\int_{X	imes Y}c(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y),\] with \(C_M:=+\infty\) if no admissible map exists. Every admissible map induces a coupling, so \(C_K\le C_M\). The relaxation has a positive gap precisely when \(C_K<C_M\). This includes the infinite-gap case where \(C_K<+\infty\) but no measurable map pushes \(\mu\) to \(
u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxation gap is positive exactly when the best coupling costs strictly less than the Monge infimum, including when finite-cost couplings exist but no admissible transport map does.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Polish spaces, \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).
\(c:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is measurable and both displayed infima are well-defined as extended-real values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive relaxation gap occurs exactly when \(C_K<C_M\).

notation.meaning: Monge optimal value, equal to positive infinity when no admissible map exists.

children.title: Transport-Map Recovery Failures
children.top_down_role: Relaxed optimizers lacking deterministic map representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport-Map Recovery Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to represent any relaxed optimizer by a deterministic map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\operatorname{Opt}_K(\mu,
u)\) denote the nonempty set of Kantorovich minimizers. Transport-map recovery fails when \[\operatorname{Opt}_K(\mu,
u)\cap igl\{(\operatorname{Id}_X,T)_\#\mu:T:X	o Y	ext{ is Borel measurable and }T_\#\mu=
u igr\}=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, for every optimal coupling, its disintegration with respect to \(\mu\) is non-Dirac on a set of positive \(\mu\)-measure. This structural failure does not by itself imply a positive value gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery fails when no optimal coupling is induced by an admissible deterministic map; equivalently, every optimal coupling splits mass on a source set of positive measure. This need not create a value gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Polish spaces with \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\) and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).
The Kantorovich problem over \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) has at least one optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transport-map recovery fails exactly when no Kantorovich optimizer equals \((\operatorname{Id}_X,T)_\#\mu\) for a Borel measurable map \(T\) satisfying \(T_\#\mu=\nu\).

children.title: Nonattained Monge Infima
children.top_down_role: Finite deterministic infima without optimizing transport maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Monge Infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite deterministic infimum approached but not realized by any map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Monge infimum is nonattained when \[C_M:=\inf_{T_\#\mu=\nu}J(T)<+\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad J(T)>C_M\ \text{for every admissible }T.\] Equivalently, for every integer \(k\ge1\), there exists an admissible map \(T_k\) such that \(J(T_k)\le C_M+1/k\), but no admissible map realizes \(C_M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Monge infimum is nonattained when admissible maps approach its value but no admissible map realizes it.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are measurable spaces, \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).
At least one measurable map \(T:X\to Y\) satisfies \(T_\#\mu=\nu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Monge infimum is nonattained exactly when every admissible \(T\) satisfies \(J(T)>C_M\), although admissible maps approach \(C_M\).

notation.meaning: Monge objective evaluated at a transport map.
Infimum of the Monge objective over admissible maps.

children.title: Linear Assignment Problems
children.top_down_role: Balanced discrete transport with one-to-one allocation structure.

assumptions_latex: Every source and target item must be matched exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The permutation problem and its linear relaxation over the doubly stochastic polytope have the same optimal value, and an optimal permutation matrix exists.

notation.meaning: Symmetric group of permutations of the item indices.
Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced one-to-one bipartite assignment and its exact linear-programming formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear assignment value admits the equivalent representations \[\min_{\sigma\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n c_{i,\sigma(i)}=\min_{X\in\mathcal B_n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij},\] where \[\mathcal B_n:=\left\{X\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times n}:\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\right\}.\] Every extreme point of \(\mathcal B_n\) is a permutation matrix; therefore the linear relaxation has an optimal permutation matrix whenever the cost entries are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-to-one assignment minimizes total pair cost. Its doubly stochastic linear relaxation is exact because the feasible polytope has permutation matrices as its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Assignment Problems

children.title: Weighted Matching Problems
children.top_down_role: Discrete transport interpreted through weighted bipartite matching.

assumptions_latex: Vertex requirements \(b_v\) and edge capacities \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
Each edge has a real cost \(w_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum-cost weighted matching is an integral feasible vector minimizing \(\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e\) under the incidence and capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost capacitated bipartite matching with prescribed vertex multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible capacitated bipartite \(b\)-matching is a vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_+^E\) satisfying \[\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=b_v\quad(v\in U\cup V),\qquad 0\le x_e\le u_e\quad(e\in E).\] The weighted matching problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:x\text{ satisfies these constraints}\right\}.\] Feasibility requires balanced total multiplicity \(\sum_{v\in U}b_v=\sum_{v\in V}b_v\), together with the capacity-compatible cut conditions imposed by \(E\) and \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted bipartite matching assigns integral edge multiplicities satisfying vertex requirements and capacities while minimizing total edge cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Matching Problems

children.title: Integral Optimizer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where optimal discrete plans occur at integral configurations.

assumptions_latex: The constraint matrix is the node-edge incidence matrix of a finite bipartite graph, possibly augmented by identity rows for integral bounds.
The right-hand side and all finite variable bounds are integral.
The linear program is feasible and has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible polyhedron has integral vertices and possesses an integral optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality supplied by bipartite incidence and integral marginal data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P:=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}.\] The bipartite node-edge incidence matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular, and adjoining signed identity rows preserves total unimodularity. Hence every vertex of \(P\) is integral when \(b\) and the finite components of \(u\) are integral. Consequently, for every cost vector \(w\in\mathbb R^E\), if \(\min_{x\in P}w^\top x\) is finite and attained, then at least one optimal solution belongs to \(\mathbb Z^E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipartite assignment relaxations have integral vertices, and therefore integral optimizers, when their requirements and capacities are integral and the incidence structure is preserved.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Optimizer Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The total-unimodularity theorem and optimizer-integrality conclusion are correctly delimited and appropriately classified, but no authoritative theorem locator is provided.

children.title: Fractional Assignment Boundary
children.top_down_role: Settings where admissible or optimal allocations require fractional mass.

assumptions_latex: Assignment variables are required to be integral in the combinatorial problem.
The linear relaxation permits nonnegative real variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonintegral marginal requirements can force fractional relaxed solutions and eliminate every integral assignment.

notation.meaning: Assignment from the single left vertex to target j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of assignment integrality when integral right-hand-side hypotheses fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one left vertex of supply \(1\) and two right vertices, each of demand \(1/2\). The relaxed balance equations are \[x_1+x_2=1,\qquad x_1=\tfrac12,\qquad x_2=\tfrac12,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.\] Their unique solution is fractional, while no solution lies in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Thus total unimodularity alone does not imply integral vertices without an integral right-hand side. More generally, additional side constraints that destroy total unimodularity can create fractional vertices even when the original marginals are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional assignments arise when marginal data are nonintegral, or when added constraints destroy total unimodularity; then the relaxed problem may have no integral feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Assignment Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly marks failure of the integral-right-hand-side hypothesis, and the side-constraint observation is properly stated as a possibility. A specific supporting source is still required.

children.title: Histogram Transport Problems
children.top_down_role: Transport between finitely supported mass histograms.

knowledge_statements.title: Histogram Transport Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite discrete optimal transport between histograms of equal total mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The histogram transport problem is \[\min_{\pi\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}\pi_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j=1}^n\pi_{ij}=a_i\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=b_j\ (1\le j\le n),\] using the convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\). A feasible matrix \(\pi\) is a discrete transport plan. If some \(c_{ij}=+\infty\), a finite-cost feasible plan must assign zero mass to those entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Histogram transport minimizes total transport cost over nonnegative matrices having the prescribed row and column sums. Infinite-cost edges must carry zero mass in every finite-cost plan.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R_+^n\) satisfy \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Discrete optimal transport minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}\pi_{ij}\) over nonnegative matrices with row sums \(a\) and column sums \(b\), with \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\).

notation.meaning: Transport matrix carrying mass from source bin i to target bin j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability Simplex and Histograms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite normalized nonnegative mass vectors, including vectors with vanishing coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), the probability simplex is \[\Sigma_n:=\left\{\mathbf a\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=1\right\}.\] An element \(\mathbf a\in\Sigma_n\) is called a histogram or probability vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive integer n, the probability simplex consists of all nonnegative n-dimensional vectors whose coordinates sum to one. Each such vector is called a histogram or probability vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Sigma_n=\left\{\mathbf a\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=1\right\},\qquad \mathbf a\in\Sigma_n\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbf a\text{ is a histogram (probability vector).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Gromov–Wasserstein Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic coupling objective for finite weighted relational spaces; arbitrary relationship matrices need not induce a genuine metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathbf a\in\mathbb R_+^n and \mathbf b\in\mathbb R_+^m have equal total mass, and let \mathbf D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n} and \mathbf D'\in\mathbb R^{m\times m} encode within-space relationships. knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Polytope Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full bipartite transportation polytope with strictly positive margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mathcal T(a,b):=\left\{\pi\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}:\sum_j\pi_{ij}=a_i,\ \sum_i\pi_{ij}=b_j\right\}.\] This set is a nonempty compact convex polytope; for example, \(\pi_{ij}=a_ib_j/M\) is strictly positive and feasible. Among the \(m+n\) marginal equalities, exactly one is redundant, so their rank is \(m+n-1\). Because a strictly positive feasible point exists, nonnegativity does not reduce the affine dimension, and \[\dim\mathcal T(a,b)=mn-(m+n-1)=(m-1)(n-1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive equal-mass margins, feasible transport matrices form a nonempty compact convex polytope of affine dimension (m−1)(n−1).
assumptions_latex: The margins have common total mass \(M:=\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transportation polytope is nonempty, compact, convex, and has affine dimension \((m-1)(n-1)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: North-West Corner Rule and Its Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the fixed-order construction, its operation and support bounds, and the family generated by row and column reorderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf a\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R_+^m\) have equal total mass. Beginning at \((i,j)=(1,1)\), assign to the current entry the minimum of the residual masses of row \(i\) and column \(j\), subtract that amount from both residuals, and advance each index whose residual becomes zero. Continuing until all mass is assigned produces, for the fixed row and column orders, a unique plan \(\operatorname{NW}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\in\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\). The construction uses at most \(n+m\) operations, its output is a vertex with at most \(n+m-1\) positive entries, and applying it after arbitrary separate row and column permutations and then undoing those permutations yields a family \(\mathcal N(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\subseteq\operatorname{ext}\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\), usually strictly contained in the full vertex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The North-West corner rule fills the current cell with the smaller residual row or column mass and advances every exhausted index. For fixed orders it uniquely produces a feasible vertex in at most n+m operations with at most n+m−1 positive entries. Reordering rows and columns generates a family that is generally only a strict subset of all vertices.
assumptions_latex: Rows and columns have fixed orders for \(\operatorname{NW}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\); reordered variants use separate row and column permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{NW}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\in\operatorname{ext}\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b),\quad |\operatorname{supp}(\operatorname{NW}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b))|\le n+m-1,\quad \mathcal N(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\subseteq\operatorname{ext}\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acyclic Support of Transportation-Polytope Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the support graph and sparsity of extreme discrete transport plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf a\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R_+^m\) have equal total mass, and let \(\mathbf P\) be an extreme point of \(\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Birkhoff theorem for the uniform transportation polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the extreme points of the uniformly normalized doubly stochastic polytope and gives the resulting deterministic-transport conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\geq1\) and \(C=\{M\in\mathbb R_+^{N\times N}:\sum_{i=1}^N M_{ij}=1/N\ \forall j,\ \sum_{j=1}^N M_{ij}=1/N\ \forall i\}\). Then \(\operatorname{ext}(C)=\{M:M_{ij}=N^{-1}\delta_{i,\sigma(j)},\ \sigma\in S_N\}\). Consequently, if \(\mu=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x_i}\) and \(\nu=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N\delta_{y_j}\), with the \(x_i\) distinct and the \(y_j\) distinct, an optimal Kantorovich plan can be chosen to be induced by a transport map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme points of the nonnegative matrix polytope having every row and column sum equal to 1/N are exactly the 1/N-scaled permutation matrices. Consequently, optimal transport between two uniform measures on N distinct atoms can be realized by a deterministic map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ext}(C)=\left\{M:M_{ij}=\frac1N\delta_{i,\sigma(j)},\ \sigma\in S_N\right\};\quad \mu=\frac1N\sum_i\delta_{x_i},\ \nu=\frac1N\sum_j\delta_{y_j}\Rightarrow\text{an optimal transport plan is induced by a map}.

children.title: Extreme-Point Transport Plans
children.top_down_role: Vertex structure and sparse representatives of transportation polytopes.

assumptions_latex: \(a\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) have equal total mass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The plan \(\pi\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal T(a,b)\) if and only if its positive-support bipartite graph is acyclic.

notation.meaning: Bipartite graph whose edges are the positive entries of the transport plan.
Transportation polytope with margins a and b.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial characterization of vertices by acyclic positive support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_\pi\) have left vertices \(1,\ldots,m\), right vertices \(1,\ldots,n\), and edge \((i,j)\) exactly when \(\pi_{ij}>0\). Then \(\pi\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal T(a,b)\) if and only if \(G_\pi\) is a forest. Consequently every extreme transport plan has at most \(m+n-1\) positive entries. A nondegenerate extreme point has exactly \(m+n-1\) positive entries, in which case its support graph is a spanning tree; degenerate extreme points have fewer positive entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport plan is a polytope vertex exactly when its positive entries contain no bipartite cycle. Thus a vertex uses at most m+n−1 transport edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Transport Plans

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forest-support characterization and support-size consequences are correct for positive margins and fit the theorem container, but no authoritative theorem or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Polytope Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial degeneracies caused by marginal mass relations.

assumptions_latex: The marginals satisfy \(a\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{m}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{n}\), and \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(a,b)\) is nondegenerate exactly when no proper nonempty index sets \(I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfy \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\).

notation.meaning: Transportation polytope with row marginal a and column marginal b.
Index sets witnessing a balanced proper subproblem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-marginal degeneracy criterion for classical transportation polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(a,b)=\{\pi\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times n}:\pi\mathbf 1=a,\ \pi^{\mathsf T}\mathbf 1=b\}\). The positive-marginal transportation polytope lies in a degenerate regime precisely when there exist proper nonempty sets \(I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). Equivalently, nondegeneracy requires every such pair to have unequal subtotal masses. In the degenerate regime, a feasible support can split along the balanced cut \(I\times J\), and some basic feasible solutions have fewer than \(m+n-1\) positive entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-marginal transportation polytope is degenerate exactly when proper row and column subsets have equal total mass.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semi-discrete transport and its Laguerre-cell representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the semi-discrete support regime and conditionally records the continuous-to-discrete cell representation, including the quadratic-cost specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\nu=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\delta_{y_i}\) be discrete and let \(\mu\) be arbitrary. Optimal transport between \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) is semi-discrete. If \(\mu\) has a density and the continuous-to-discrete transport is represented by an optimal map, then, up to \(\mu\)-null sets, the source is partitioned into disjoint cells \(L_i\) mapped to the atoms \(y_i\). For \(c(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert^2\), these cells are Laguerre cells, equivalently weighted Voronoi or power-diagram cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transport is semi-discrete when one measure is discrete and the other is arbitrary. When a continuous source is transported to discrete target atoms through an optimal map, the source is partitioned, up to null sets, into cells assigned to those atoms. Under squared Euclidean cost, the cells are Laguerre cells, also known as weighted Voronoi or power-diagram cells.

\text{the transport is represented by an optimal map for the map-induced cell conclusion}
c(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert^2\text{ for the Laguerre-cell conclusion}

children.title: Laguerre Cell Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Weighted cell partitions arising in semi-discrete transport.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cells \(L_i(w)\) cover \(X\), and their interiors are pairwise disjoint.

notation.meaning: Laguerre cell associated with site i and weight vector w.

review_flags: Standard semi-discrete transport definition; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-cost Laguerre decomposition restricted to the source domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), define the Laguerre cell
\[
L_i(w)=\bigl\{x\in X:\lVert x-y_i\rVert^2-w_i\leq \lVert x-y_j\rVert^2-w_j\ \text{for every }j\bigr\}.
\]
Then \(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^N L_i(w)\), and the interiors of distinct cells are disjoint. A point belongs to several cells exactly when the minimum weighted squared distance is attained by several sites. Thus \(\{L_i(w)\}_{i=1}^N\) is a closed-cell decomposition, modulo its shared boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Laguerre cells assign each source point to sites minimizing weighted squared distance; they cover the domain with disjoint interiors.
knowledge_statements.title: Laguerre Cell Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. Moreover, pairwise-disjoint interiors require an appropriate full-dimensional or relative-interior setting; for arbitrary X contained in a tie hyperplane, distinct cells can have overlapping relative interiors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Laguerre Cells and the Constant-Weight Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and covering property of semi-discrete Laguerre cells, including the failure of literal disjointness at ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\), let \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\in\mathcal Y\), and let \(\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^m\). Define
\[
\mathbb L_{\mathbf g}(y_j):=\left\{x\in\mathcal X: c(x,y_j)-g_j\le c(x,y_{j'})-g_{j'}\ \text{for every }j'\ne j\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal X=\bigcup_{j=1}^m\mathbb L_{\mathbf g}(y_j).
\]
The cells are disjoint at points having a unique minimizing index; ties can place a point in multiple cells unless a tie-breaking convention is imposed. If \(\mathbf g\) is constant, these cells are the unweighted \(c\)-Voronoi cells. They coincide with the ordinary Euclidean Voronoi cells when ordering by \(c(x,y)\) is equivalent to ordering by Euclidean distance, as for Euclidean distance or squared Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Laguerre cell contains the points for which one site's cost minus its weight is minimal. The cells cover the source space, but ties can make their closed-cell definitions overlap unless minimizers are unique or ties are broken. Constant weights recover the unweighted cost-Voronoi cells and, for Euclidean distance-type costs, the ordinary Voronoi diagram.
assumptions_latex: Literal disjointness requires unique minimizing indices or an explicit tie-breaking convention.
The ordinary Euclidean Voronoi specialization requires that comparison by \(c(x,y)\) agree with comparison by Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal X=\bigcup_{j=1}^m\mathbb L_{\mathbf g}(y_j)\); uniqueness or tie-breaking yields a disjoint decomposition, while constant weights yield unweighted \(c\)-Voronoi cells.

children.title: Power-Diagram Representation
children.top_down_role: Euclidean weighted-diagram representation of semi-discrete transport cells.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each Laguerre cell is the intersection of \(X\) with a power-diagram cell having power weights \(w_i\).

notation.meaning: Affine score equivalent to weighted squared distance.

review_flags: Standard computational-geometry representation; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine half-space representation of quadratic Laguerre cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Expanding the quadratic terms gives
\[
\lVert x-y_i\rVert^2-w_i\leq\lVert x-y_j\rVert^2-w_j
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2\langle x,y_i-y_j\rangle\geq \lVert y_i\rVert^2-w_i-\lVert y_j\rVert^2+w_j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
L_i(w)=X\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^N\bigl\{x:2\langle x,y_i-y_j\rangle\geq \lVert y_i\rVert^2-w_i-\lVert y_j\rVert^2+w_j\bigr\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(L_i(w)=\{x\in X:s_i(x)\geq s_j(x)\ \text{for all }j\}\), where \(s_i(x)=2\langle x,y_i\rangle-\lVert y_i\rVert^2+w_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding weighted squared distances represents every Laguerre cell as an intersection of affine half-spaces, hence as a power-diagram cell.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Diagram Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The half-space expansion and representation content kind fit the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mass map obeys \(M(w+t\mathbf 1)=M(w)\), \(\sum_iM_i(w)=\mu(X)\), and \(\partial M_i/\partial w_j=-\int_{F_{ij}(w)}\rho/(2\lVert y_i-y_j\rVert)\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}\) for \(i\ne j\).

notation.meaning: Common interface between cells i and j.

review_flags: Differentiability formula requires regular interfaces and trace regularity of the density.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mass-map invariance and facet derivative in a regular Laguerre regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(M_i(w)=\mu(L_i(w))\). Then \(M(w+t\mathbf 1)=M(w)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^N M_i(w)=\mu(X)\). At a weight vector where all relevant interfaces are regular and differentiation under moving facets is valid, for \(i\ne j\),
\[
\frac{\partial M_i}{\partial w_j}(w)=-\int_{F_{ij}(w)}\frac{\rho(x)}{2\lVert y_i-y_j\rVert}\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).
\]
The diagonal derivative satisfies \(\partial M_i/\partial w_i=-\sum_{j\ne i}\partial M_i/\partial w_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cell masses conserve total mass, ignore common weight shifts, and vary across shared facets according to weighted interface area.
knowledge_statements.title: Cell-Mass Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The invariance and conservation claims are standard, but the facet-derivative formula needs precise geometric and density regularity assumptions and an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regular cell-mass calculus fails at weights \(w\) when a tie set \(B_{ij}(w)\) has positive \(\mu\)-mass, when a cell is created or disappears with nonregular contact, or when several interfaces meet nontransversally on a set carrying relevant boundary measure. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\nu=\sum_{i=1}^N b_i\delta_{y_i}\), where \(b_i>0\) and \(\sum_i b_i=1\). Define
\[
D(w)=\sum_{i=1}^N b_iw_i+\int_X\min_{1\leq i\leq N}\bigl(c(x,y_i)-w_i\bigr)\,d\mu(x).
\]
Under hypotheses ensuring Kantorovich duality and attainment of the displayed integrals,
\[
\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times\{y_i\}}c(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y)=\sup_{w\in\mathbb{R}^N}D(w).
\]
If ties have zero \(\mu\)-mass, then \(D\) is differentiable and \(\partial D/\partial w_i=b_i-\mu(L_i(w))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Semi-Discrete Transport Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of the transport cost when the target marginal has finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}\) and
\[
\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x)=\min_{1\le j\le m}\bigl(c(x,y_j)-g_j\bigr).
\]
Under the hypotheses of the semi-discrete Kantorovich dual formulation,
\[
\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)=\max_{\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^m}\mathcal E(\mathbf g),
\qquad
\mathcal E(\mathbf g):=\int_{\mathcal X}\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x)\,d\alpha(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m b_jg_j.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the target measure is supported on m points, the semi-discrete Kantorovich dual is a finite-dimensional maximization over one weight per target point. The objective is the source integral of the discrete backward cost transform plus the target-weighted sum of those weights.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entropic semi-discrete dual representation and gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the entropic dual, smoothed cost transforms, and their finite-dimensional semi-discrete specialization, including the stated unregularized boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\varepsilon>0\), the entropic dual is
\[
\mathcal L_c^\varepsilon(\alpha,\beta)=\max_{(f,g)\in\mathcal C(\mathcal X)\times\mathcal C(\mathcal Y)}\left\{\int_{\mathcal X}f\,d\alpha+\int_{\mathcal Y}g\,d\beta-\varepsilon\int_{\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y}e^{(f(x)+g(y)-c(x,y))/\varepsilon}\,d\alpha(x)d\beta(y)\right\}.
\]
Elimination of either potential defines
\[
f^{c,\varepsilon}(y)=-\varepsilon\log\int_{\mathcal X}e^{(-c(x,y)+f(x))/\varepsilon}\,d\alpha(x),\qquad g^{\bar c,\varepsilon}(x)=-\varepsilon\log\int_{\mathcal Y}e^{(-c(x,y)+g(y))/\varepsilon}\,d\beta(y).
\]
If \(\beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}\), then
\[
g^{\bar c,\varepsilon}(x)=-\varepsilon\log\sum_{j=1}^m b_j e^{(-c(x,y_j)+g_j)/\varepsilon},\qquad \max_{g\in\mathbb R^m}\mathcal E^\varepsilon(g),\quad \mathcal E^\varepsilon(g)=\int_{\mathcal X}g^{\bar c,\varepsilon}(x)\,d\alpha(x)-\langle g,b\rangle .
\]
The alternating discrete updates are \(f_i^{(\ell+1)}=g^{\bar c,\varepsilon}(x_i)\) and \(g_j^{(\ell+1)}=f^{c,\varepsilon}(y_j)\). Moreover, for every \(j\in\llbracket m\rrbracket\),
\[
\nabla\mathcal E^\varepsilon(g)_j=-\int_{\mathcal X}\chi_j^\varepsilon(x)\,d\alpha(x)+b_j,\qquad \chi_j^\varepsilon(x)=\frac{e^{(-c(x,y_j)+g_j)/\varepsilon}}{\sum_\ell e^{(-c(x,y_\ell)+g_\ell)/\varepsilon}},
\]
with \(\chi_j^\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(\sum_j\chi_j^\varepsilon=1\). The finite-dimensional objective and gradient formula extend to \(\varepsilon=0\), where \(g^{\bar c,0}=g^{\bar c}\) and \(\chi_j^0\) is the indicator of the corresponding Laguerre cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropic optimal transport has a smooth unconstrained dual whose elimination of either potential produces a log-sum-exp smoothed cost transform. When the target measure has finitely many atoms, this yields a finite-dimensional semi-discrete dual objective. Its gradient is the difference between the target masses and the source masses assigned by nonnegative soft Laguerre-cell functions forming a partition of unity. The alternating transforms give the corresponding Sinkhorn updates, and the stated objective and gradient extend to zero regularization using ordinary cost transforms and Laguerre-cell indicators.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are measures on \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\), and the displayed integrals are well defined.
\(\varepsilon>0\) for the entropic logarithmic transforms; the unregularized boundary is interpreted at \(\varepsilon=0\).
For the semi-discrete specialization, \(\beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}\) and \(g\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L_c^\varepsilon\) admits the displayed smoothed-transform reduction to \(\max_g\mathcal E^\varepsilon(g)\), with \(\nabla\mathcal E^\varepsilon(g)_j=-\int\chi_j^\varepsilon\,d\alpha+b_j\), \(\chi_j^\varepsilon\ge0\), \(\sum_j\chi_j^\varepsilon=1\), and the stated \(\varepsilon=0\) extension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Backward Cost Transform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support backward cost transform used in semi-discrete transport duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\) and \(\beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}\). For \(\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^m\), its discrete \(\bar c\)-transform is
\[
\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x):=\min_{1\le j\le m}\bigl(c(x,y_j)-g_j\bigr),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.
\]
This is the ordinary \(\bar c\)-transform with minimization restricted to the finite support of \(\beta\). If \(c(\cdot,y_j)\) is continuous for every \(j\), then \(\mathbf g^{\bar c}\in C(\mathcal X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finitely supported target measure, the discrete backward cost transform of a vector g is the pointwise minimum of c(x,y_j)-g_j over the target sites. It is the ordinary transform restricted to those sites and is continuous when each cost function c(·,y_j) is continuous.
assumptions_latex: For the continuity conclusion, \(c(\cdot,y_j)\in C(\mathcal X)\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x)=\min_{1\le j\le m}(c(x,y_j)-g_j)\); under the stated continuity assumption, \(\mathbf g^{\bar c}\in C(\mathcal X)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected stochastic supergradient ascent for the finite-dimensional dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input sites \(y_i\), target masses \(b_i\), steps \(\eta_k>0\), and samples \(X_k\sim\mu\). Initialize \(w^0\in H=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^N:\sum_iw_i=0\}\). For \(k\geq0\), choose
\[
I_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq i\leq N}\bigl(c(X_k,y_i)-w_i^k\bigr),\qquad g_k=b-e_{I_k},
\]
and update \(w^{k+1}=\operatorname{proj}_H(w^k+\eta_kg_k)\). Stop after \(K\) samples and output the weighted average \(\bar w_K=(\sum_{k<K}\eta_kw^k)/(\sum_{k<K}\eta_k)\), or stop earlier when an empirical mass residual is below a prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the source, assign each sample to its cheapest weighted site, and ascend the dual using target mass minus sampled assignment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radon Transform of a Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the transform through all one-dimensional projection marginals, including its density representation and the Radon–X-ray dimensional boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(\pi_e(x)=x\cdot e\) for each \(e\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\), and set \(\mu_e=(\pi_e)_\#\mu\). The Radon transform is the family \(R\mu=(\mu_e)_{e\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\). If \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous, then every \(\mu_e\) is absolutely continuous, so \(\mu_e=f_e(t)\,dt\) and \(R\mu(e,t)=f_e(t)\). In dimensions \(d>2\), projection onto hyperplanes gives the distinct X-ray transform; the Radon and X-ray transforms coincide when \(d=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Radon transform of a measure is its family of pushforwards under all scalar projections. For an absolutely continuous measure, every projected measure has a density, which represents the transform as a function. Radon and X-ray transforms coincide in dimension two but are distinct constructions in higher dimensions.
assumptions_latex: For the density representation, \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\mu=(\mu_e)_{e\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}},\qquad \mu_e=(\pi_e)_\#\mu;\quad \mu\ll dx\Rightarrow \mu_e=f_e(t)\,dt\text{ and }R\mu(e,t)=f_e(t).

children.title: Atomic Source Regime
children.top_down_role: Transport problems whose source measure contains point masses.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Polish space and \(\mu\) is a finite Borel measure on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The source is purely atomic exactly when \(\mu=\sum_{k\in K}a_k\delta_{x_k}\) for an at most countable set of distinct points with \(a_k>0\).

notation.meaning: At most countable atom index set.

review_flags: Standard measure-theoretic definition; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely atomic finite source measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite Borel source measure \(\mu\) on a Polish space \(X\) is in the purely atomic regime when there exist an at most countable index set \(K\), distinct points \(x_k\in X\), and masses \(a_k>0\) such that
\[
\mu=\sum_{k\in K}a_k\delta_{x_k},\qquad \sum_{k\in K}a_k=\mu(X).
\]
Equivalently, every measurable set of positive \(\mu\)-mass contains a \(\mu\)-atom. Transport plans may split each mass \(a_k\), whereas a deterministic map must send the entire atom at \(x_k\) to one image point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A purely atomic source is a finite or countable weighted sum of Dirac masses; deterministic maps cannot split any source atom.
knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Source Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the atomic-source leaf, but the countable representation and stated equivalence have no cited measure-theory source.

children.title: Singular Nonatomic Source Regime
children.top_down_role: Sources singular to volume measure without atomic concentration.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is Borel and \(\mu\) is a finite Borel measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is characterized by \(\mu\perp\mathcal L^d\) and \(\mu(\{x\})=0\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: A Lebesgue-null carrier of the source.

review_flags: Standard measure decomposition terminology; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomless measures singular with respect to ambient Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite Borel source measure \(\mu\) on \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is singular nonatomic when
\[
\mu\perp\mathcal L^d
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mu(\{x\})=0\ \text{for every }x\in X.
\]
Thus there is a Borel set \(S\subset X\) with \(\mathcal L^d(S)=0\) and \(\mu(X\setminus S)=0\), but no singleton has positive mass. This regime includes measures distributed continuously on lower-dimensional sets and does not satisfy the ambient absolute-continuity hypothesis used in the standard Euclidean quadratic-map theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular nonatomic source lives on a Lebesgue-null set but assigns zero mass to every individual point.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Nonatomic Source Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly targets the singular nonatomic regime, but no inspectable source supports the terminology and characterization.

children.title: Mixed Source Regime
children.top_down_role: Sources combining atomic, singular, or absolutely continuous components.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is Borel and \(\mu\) is a finite Borel measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed regime has both a nonzero atomic component \(\mu_{\mathrm{at}}\) and a nonzero nonatomic component \(\mu_{\mathrm{na}}\).

notation.meaning: Purely atomic component of the source.
Mass of the atom at x.

review_flags: Standard atomic–nonatomic decomposition; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical mixture of atomic and atomless source components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every finite Borel measure \(\mu\) admits the decomposition
\[
\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{at}}+\mu_{\mathrm{na}},
\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm{at}}=\sum_{x:\,\mu(\{x\})>0}\mu(\{x\})\delta_x,
\]
where \(\mu_{\mathrm{na}}(\{x\})=0\) for every \(x\). The source lies in the mixed regime when \(\mu_{\mathrm{at}}(X)>0\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{na}}(X)>0\). The nonatomic component may itself have absolutely continuous and singular parts; the defining feature here is coexistence of indivisible source atoms with atomless mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed source has both positive atomic mass and positive atomless mass; its atomless part may be absolutely continuous or singular.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Source Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomic–nonatomic decomposition fits the mixed-source leaf, but the canonical decomposition and countability implicit in the atomic sum require a cited measure-theory locator.

children.title: Deterministic Transport Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on map existence caused by singular source structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are measurable spaces, \(T:X\to Y\) is measurable, and \(\mu\) has an atom \(x_0\) of mass \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every deterministic pushforward \(T_\#\mu\) has an atom of mass at least \(a\) at \(T(x_0)\); hence it cannot equal an atomless target.
review_flags: Elementary pushforward obstruction; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic obstruction to deterministic transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x_0\) is a source atom with \(a=\mu(\{x_0\})>0\), then every measurable map \(T:X\to Y\) satisfies
\[
(T_\#\mu)(\{T(x_0)\})=\mu(T^{-1}(\{T(x_0)\}))\geq a.
\]
Therefore no deterministic map can push a measure having an atom onto an atomless target. More generally, deterministic transport cannot subdivide any source atom: each atomic mass must be assigned wholly to one target point, possibly together with other source mass. Kantorovich plans cross this boundary because they may split the mass at \(x_0\) among several destinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic map sends each source atom intact, so any atomic source cannot map to an atomless target; transport plans may split it.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Transport Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomic pushforward obstruction is mathematically precise and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no authoritative transport or measure-theory source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique map-induced transport for mutually singular marginals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Monge existence and uniqueness result for mutually singular probability measures and strictly concave distance costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mu and \nu be mutually singular probability measures on \mathbb{R}^d with \mu\ll\mathcal{L}^d. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recursive Definition of the Knothe–Rosenblatt Rearrangement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extracted target-conditional index is typographically damaged; the statement records the unambiguous recursive dependence on the already transported trailing coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given source and target probability densities \(f,g\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), define \(T^d:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) as the monotone nondecreasing transport from the last marginal \(f^d\) to \(g^d\). Recursively for \(k=d-1,\ldots,1\), after defining \(T^j\) for \(j>k\), let \(T^k(x_k,\ldots,x_d)\) be the monotone nondecreasing transport in \(x_k\) from the source conditional density indexed by \((x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d)\) to the target conditional density indexed by \(\widehat T^{k+1}(x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d)\). Set \[\widehat T^k(x_k,\ldots,x_d)=\bigl(T^k(x_k,\ldots,x_d),T^{k+1}(x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d),\ldots,T^d(x_d)\bigr).\] The Knothe–Rosenblatt rearrangement is \(T=\widehat T^1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Knothe–Rosenblatt map is built backward through the coordinates. Each component monotonically transports a one-dimensional conditional source distribution to the corresponding target conditional distribution, using the already transported later coordinates as parameters.

children.title: Atomic Quantile Jumps
children.top_down_role: Discontinuities in quantile representations caused by atoms.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R\).
\(Q_\mu\) is the generalized inverse of the right-continuous distribution function \(F_\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(\{x\})=a>0\) exactly when \(Q_\mu=x\) on a parameter interval of length \(a\).

notation.meaning: Left limit of the distribution function.
Mass of the atom at the point.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atoms create CDF jumps and quantile plateaus, not quantile jumps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\mu(\{x\})=F_\mu(x)-F_\mu(x-).
\]
Consequently, \(x\) is an atom of mass \(a>0\) if and only if
\[
Q_\mu(u)=x\quad\text{for almost every }u\in(F_\mu(x-),F_\mu(x)],
\]
whose length is \(a\). Thus an atomic jump of \(F_\mu\) corresponds under generalized inversion to a constant quantile interval. A discontinuous jump of \(Q_\mu\), by contrast, records a gap in the support rather than an atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom of mass a is a jump of the CDF and produces a constant quantile interval of length a; quantile jumps instead reflect support gaps.
knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Quantile Jumps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly distinguishes CDF jumps caused by atoms from quantile jumps caused by support gaps. This terminological interpretation of the immutable title requires an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Tie Intervals
children.top_down_role: Intervals or level sets permitting multiple monotone allocations.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive-length level interval of \(Q_\mu\) exists exactly at an atom of \(\mu\), and its length equals the atomic mass.

notation.meaning: Parameter interval on which the quantile is tied at one value.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tie intervals are level sets of a generalized quantile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R\), define \(I_x=(F_\mu(x-),F_\mu(x)]\). Then
\[
Q_\mu(u)=x\quad\text{for every }u\in I_x,
\qquad |I_x|=\mu(\{x\}).
\]
Conversely, if \(Q_\mu(u)=x\) almost everywhere on an interval \(I\subset(0,1)\) of positive length, then \(I\subseteq I_x\) up to endpoints and \(\mu(\{x\})\ge |I|>0\). Hence positive-length tie intervals occur precisely because the transported measure has atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantile has a positive-length tie interval exactly at an atom; the maximal interval length equals that atom's mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Tie Intervals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atom–quantile-level-interval characterization is precise, and condition is a suitable content kind. No supporting source or locator is provided.

children.title: Nonunique Monotone Maps
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of deterministic monotone transports.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu,\nu\) are Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R\).
Maps are required to be Borel and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotone pushforward maps are unique \(\mu\)-almost everywhere when they exist; atoms can instead prevent existence, while pointwise representatives remain nonunique on \(\mu\)-null sets.

notation.meaning: Pushforward of the source measure by a map.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes representative nonuniqueness from failure of map existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If nondecreasing maps \(S,T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(S_\#\mu=T_\#\mu=\nu\), then \(S=T\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere. They may nevertheless differ on \(\mu\)-null sets, so pointwise representatives are nonunique. More substantially, if \(x\) is a source atom of mass \(a>0\), every deterministic map sends its entire mass to the single atom \(T(x)\); therefore \(T_\#\mu=\nu\) is impossible whenever no target atom can receive that indivisible mass consistently. In such cases the monotone quantile coupling generally splits the atom and is not induced by a map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existing monotone pushforward maps are unique almost everywhere. Apparent nonuniqueness is null-set freedom; source atoms can instead force splitting and destroy map existence.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Monotone Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between null-set representative freedom and failure of deterministic-map existence is plausible and fits a failure boundary, but the phrase about a target atom receiving mass 'consistently' is not a precise compatibility condition. The immutable title also makes the intended notion of nonuniqueness ambiguous. A source is needed to settle the intended formulation.

children.title: Unique-Map Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Source-target configurations that remove atomic or tie-driven ambiguity.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu,\nu\) are Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=Q_\nu\circ F_\mu\) pushes \(\mu\) to \(\nu\) and is the unique nondecreasing pushforward map \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomless-source recovery of the deterministic monotone rearrangement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(\mu\) is atomless, \(F_\mu\) is continuous and \((F_\mu)_\#\mu\) is the uniform probability measure on \((0,1)\). Hence the map
\[
T(x)=Q_\nu(F_\mu(x))
\]
is Borel, nondecreasing, and satisfies \(T_\#\mu=\nu\). If \(S:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is any other nondecreasing Borel map with \(S_\#\mu=\nu\), then \(S=T\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere. For costs \(c(x,y)=h(x-y)\) with \(h\) convex, the induced coupling \((\mathrm{id},T)_\#\mu\) is optimal whenever its cost is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an atomless source, composing its CDF with the target quantile gives the unique almost-everywhere monotone transport map.
knowledge_statements.title: Unique-Map Recovery Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomless-source monotone rearrangement theorem and its convex displacement-cost qualification are standard and appropriately placed, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Metric-Cost Transport
children.top_down_role: Static transport problems using an underlying metric as cost.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum transport cost for \(c=d\) is \(W_1(\mu,\nu)\).

notation.meaning: Couplings of the two probability measures.
Probability measures with finite first moment.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static optimal transport with the ambient metric as cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric-cost transport is the Kantorovich problem with \(c(x,y)=d(x,y)\):
\[
\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y).
\]
The finite-first-moment assumptions make this value finite, and lower semicontinuity of \(d\) ensures that the infimum is attained. Its value is, by definition, \(W_1(\mu,\nu)\). Unlike strictly convex displacement costs, the metric cost is only linear along distance-minimizing directions and may admit several optimal couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric-cost transport minimizes expected distance over all couplings. For finite-first-moment measures, its attained value is the one-Wasserstein distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Cost Transport

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and attainment statement are correct for finite-first-moment measures on a Polish metric space, and definition fits the terminal container. No supporting transport reference is supplied.

children.title: One-Wasserstein Geometry
children.top_down_role: Metric geometry associated with first-order transport cost.

assumptions_latex: A base point \(x_0\in X\) is fixed, and measures lie in \(\mathcal P_1(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_1\) is a metric on \(\mathcal P_1(X)\) and metrizes weak convergence together with convergence of first moments.

notation.meaning: Probability measures having finite first moment.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric and convergence structure induced by expected distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(W_1:\mathcal P_1(X)\times\mathcal P_1(X)\to[0,\infty)\) is a metric. In particular, it is symmetric, obeys the triangle inequality, and \(W_1(\mu,\nu)=0\) holds exactly when \(\mu=\nu\). Moreover,
\[
W_1(\mu_n,\mu)\to0
\]
if and only if \(\mu_n\rightharpoonup\mu\) and
\[
\int_X d(x,x_0)\,d\mu_n(x)\to\int_X d(x,x_0)\,d\mu(x).
\]
The characterization is independent of the chosen base point \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-Wasserstein distance is a genuine metric, and its convergence is exactly weak convergence plus convergence of first moments.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Wasserstein Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric and convergence characterization is standard and matches the container, but it lacks an authoritative citation with a section, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Lipschitz Dual Potentials
children.top_down_role: Dual-potential geometry characteristic of metric transport costs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_1(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1}\int_X f\,d(\mu-\nu)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz seminorm of a real-valued function.
Signed difference of the two measures.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality for metric cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The metric-cost transport value admits the dual representation
\[
W_1(\mu,\nu)=\sup\left\{\int_X f\,d\mu-\int_X f\,d\nu: f:X\to\mathbb R,\ \operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1\right\}.
\]
Adding a constant to \(f\) does not change the objective, so one may impose \(f(x_0)=0\) at any fixed \(x_0\in X\). If an optimal coupling \(\pi\) and an optimal potential \(f\) exist, complementary slackness gives \(f(x)-f(y)=d(x,y)\) for \(\pi\)-almost every \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-Wasserstein distance equals the largest expectation difference over all real-valued 1-Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Dual Potentials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Kantorovich–Rubinstein formula and conditional complementary-slackness statement are internally consistent with the stated sign convention. No inspectable source with a precise locator is supplied.

children.title: Nondifferentiable Cost Boundary
children.top_down_role: Map-structure limitations caused by nonsmooth metric costs.

assumptions_latex: The cost is \(c(x,y)=\|x-y\|\) on a normed vector space.
Differentiability is considered with respect to either transport variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric cost is nondifferentiable on the diagonal and lacks the strict convexity needed for standard smooth quadratic-cost map arguments.

notation.meaning: Diagonal where source and target positions coincide.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness boundary separating metric and quadratic costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(c(x,y)=\|x-y\|\), the cost is generally nondifferentiable when \(x=y\). In Euclidean space,
\[
\partial_x c(x,y)=\left\{\frac{x-y}{\|x-y\|}\right\}\quad\text{if }x\ne y,
\qquad
\partial_x c(x,x)=\{v:\|v\|\le1\}.
\]
Furthermore, displacement homogeneity makes \(c\) non-strictly convex along rays. Therefore arguments relying on a single-valued smooth cost gradient or strict convexity—such as direct quadratic-cost recovery of a unique transport map—can fail, even though Kantorovich duality and optimal couplings remain available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance cost is nonsmooth on the diagonal and non-strictly convex along rays, so smooth quadratic-cost arguments for unique maps do not directly apply.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondifferentiable Cost Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Euclidean subdifferential formula and the identified smoothness and strict-convexity boundary are appropriate for a failure-boundary record. An authoritative source with a precise locator is missing.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Transport Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean Brenier theorem for absolutely continuous source measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists a convex lower-semicontinuous function \(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) whose gradient \(T=\nabla\varphi\) is defined \(\mu\)-almost everywhere and satisfies \(T_\#\mu=\nu\). The coupling
\[
\pi=(\mathrm{id},T)_\#\mu
\]
is the unique minimizer in \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) of
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2\,d\pi(x,y).
\]
Consequently, the optimal quadratic transport is induced by a map \(T\) that is unique \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic Euclidean cost and an absolutely continuous source, the unique optimal coupling is induced by the almost-everywhere unique gradient map of a convex function.
assumptions_latex: The source measure \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(c(x,y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2\), the unique optimal plan is \((\mathrm{id},\nabla\varphi)_\#\mu\) for a convex \(\varphi\), and \(\nabla\varphi\) is unique \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.

notation.meaning: Identity map on the source space.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) are open and \(c\in C^1(X\times Y)\).
For every \(x\in X\), the map \(y\mapsto\nabla_xc(x,y)\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At differentiability points of an active dual potential, the twist condition determines the paired target uniquely.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical source-side twist condition for smooth costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cost \(c\) satisfies the source twist condition when
\[
y_1\ne y_2\implies \nabla_xc(x,y_1)\ne\nabla_xc(x,y_2)
\]
for every fixed \(x\in X\). If dual potentials satisfy \(\phi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)\), equality holds at \((x,y)\), and \(\phi\) is differentiable at \(x\), then
\[
\nabla\phi(x)=\nabla_xc(x,y).
\]
By twist, this equation has at most one solution \(y\). Thus an optimal plan concentrated on the equality set is induced by a map wherever the source potential is differentiable, subject to the usual existence hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth cost is twisted when its source gradient identifies the target uniquely; then differentiable dual potentials determine a transport map.
knowledge_statements.title: General Twisted Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The source twist condition, dual sign convention, and local uniqueness conclusion are consistent. The condition content kind fits, but the map-level consequence and its usual auxiliary hypotheses require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave distance transport costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the cost class and records the metric consequences, including the boundary cases for strictness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \ell:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}_+ be increasing and concave, and define c(x,y)=\ell(|x-y|). Such costs are subadditive. If \ell(0)=0, then c satisfies the triangle inequality and defines a distance on \mathbb{R}^d. If \ell is strictly concave, then \ell(a+b)<\ell(a)+\ell(b) for a,b>0, so c(x,z)<c(x,y)+c(y,z) whenever x\ne y and y\ne z.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave distance transport cost has the form c(x,y)=ell(|x-y|), with ell increasing and concave. It is subadditive; when ell(0)=0 it is a metric. Strict concavity gives a strict triangle inequality whenever both legs have positive length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell(0)=0\implies c(x,z)\le c(x,y)+c(y,z),\quad \ell\text{ strictly concave and }x\ne y\ne z\implies c(x,z)<c(x,y)+c(y,z).

children.title: Repulsive Transport Costs
children.top_down_role: Costs favoring separation rather than proximity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing \(I_c\) penalizes mass concentrated near the diagonal \(\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in X\}\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-marginal radial repulsion with a singular collision penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the repulsive transport cost \(c:X\times X\to[0,+\infty]\) by
\[
c(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
h(d(x,y)),&x\ne y,\\+\infty,&x=y.
\end{cases}
\]
For probability measures \(\mu,\nu\), its transport problem minimizes \(I_c(\gamma)=\int c\,d\gamma\) over \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\). Because \(h\) is nonincreasing, pairs at larger separation have no greater cost; because \(h(r)\to+\infty\) as \(r\downarrow0\), collisions and near-collisions are penalized. In particular, every finite-cost coupling satisfies \(\gamma(\Delta)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repulsive cost decreases with separation and diverges at collisions, so every finite-cost coupling avoids the diagonal.

knowledge_statements.title: Forbidden-Configuration Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard pairwise exclusions encoded by an infinite-valued cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be measurable spaces, let \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), \(
u\in\mathcal P(Y)\), let \(F\subseteq X	imes Y\) be measurable, and let \(c_0:X	imes Y	o[0,+\infty)\) be measurable. Define \(\iota_{F^c}:X	imes Y	o\{0,+\infty\}\) by \(\iota_{F^c}=0\) on \(F^c\) and \(\iota_{F^c}=+\infty\) on \(F\), and set \(c:=c_0+\iota_{F^c}\). Then, for every \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,
u)\), \[\int c\,d\gamma<+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma(F)=0\ 	ext{ and }\ \int c_0\,d\gamma<+\infty.\] Moreover, \[\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,
u)}\int c\,d\gamma=\inf_{\substack{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,
u)\ \gamma(F)=0}}\int c_0\,d\gamma,\] with \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding an infinite indicator of a measurable forbidden set is equivalent to restricting transport to couplings that assign that set zero mass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-cost transport for \(c=c_0+\iota_{F^c}\) is transport constrained by \(\gamma(F)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Double c-Transform Characterization of c-Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes c-convex functions as fixed points of c-convexification under the chapter's c-transform conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\psi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \[\psi^{cc}(x)=(\psi^c)^c(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}\inf_{\widetilde x\in\mathcal X}\bigl(\psi(\widetilde x)+c(\widetilde x,y)-c(x,y)\bigr).\] Then \[\psi\text{ is }c\text{-convex}\iff \psi^{cc}=\psi.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is c-convex exactly when applying the c-transform twice leaves it unchanged.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: c-Convexity, c-Transform, and c-Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the primal-side potential calculus for an arbitrary extended-real transport cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) be sets and \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). A function \(\psi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is \(c\)-convex if \(\psi\not\equiv+\infty\) and there exists \(\zeta:\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\) such that \[\psi(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}\bigl(\zeta(y)-c(x,y)\bigr)\quad\forall x\in\mathcal X.\] Its \(c\)-transform is \[\psi^c(y)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\bigl(\psi(x)+c(x,y)\bigr),\] and its \(c\)-subdifferential is \[\partial_c\psi=\{(x,y)\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y:\psi^c(y)-\psi(x)=c(x,y)\}.\] The functions \(\psi\) and \(\psi^c\) are \(c\)-conjugate, \(\partial_c\psi\) is \(c\)-cyclically monotone, and \[y\in\partial_c\psi(x)\iff \psi(x)+c(x,y)\leq\psi(z)+c(z,y)\quad\forall z\in\mathcal X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nontrivial function is c-convex when it is a supremum of translates of the negative cost. Its c-transform minimizes the function plus cost; equality defines the c-subdifferential, whose graph is c-cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi\text{ is }c\text{-convex}\iff \exists\zeta\ \forall x,\ \psi(x)=\sup_y(\zeta(y)-c(x,y));\quad \psi^c(y)=\inf_x(\psi(x)+c(x,y));\quad y\in\partial_c\psi(x)\iff\forall z,\ \psi(x)+c(x,y)\leq\psi(z)+c(z,y),\quad \partial_c\psi\text{ is }c\text{-cyclically monotone}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strassen coupling theorem at tolerance \(\varepsilon\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual characterization of the minimum probability that a coupling exceeds a prescribed metric tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,d)\) be a Polish metric space, let \(\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge 0\). For \(A\subseteq X\), set \(A^{\varepsilon}:=\{y\in X:d(y,A)\le\varepsilon\}\), where \(d(y,A):=\inf_{z\in A}d(y,z)\). Then
\[
\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\pi\bigl(\{(x,y):d(x,y)>\varepsilon\}\bigr)=\sup_{A\subseteq X,\ A\text{ closed}}\bigl\{\mu(A)-\nu(A^{\varepsilon})\bigr\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two probability measures on a Polish metric space, the smallest probability under any coupling that the paired points are more than ε apart equals the largest difference μ(A)−ν(A^ε) over closed sets A, where A^ε is the closed ε-neighborhood of A.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\pi\{(x,y):d(x,y)>\varepsilon\}=\sup_{A\subseteq X,\ A\text{ closed}}\{\mu(A)-\nu(A^{\varepsilon})\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: c-monotone set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-dependent cyclical monotonicity under every finite permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \Gamma\subset X\times Y is c\text{-monotone} if, for every n\ge1, every (x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\in\Gamma, and every permutation \sigma of \{1,\ldots,n\},\quad \sum_{i=1}^n c(x_i,y_{\sigma(i)})\ge\sum_{i=1}^n c(x_i,y_i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of the transport product space is c-monotone when no finite permutation of the selected y-coordinates lowers the total cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^n c(x_i,y_{\sigma(i)})\ge\sum_{i=1}^n c(x_i,y_i)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of dual optimal potentials for a fixed continuous cost on compact metric spaces under weak convergence of both marginals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposition of Nonnegative Linear Forms on Bounded Continuous Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposes a nonnegative linear form into its measure component and a component supported at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be locally compact, \(\sigma\)-compact Polish spaces. If \(\ell\) is a nonnegative linear form on \(C_b(X\times Y)\), then
\[
\ell=\pi+R,
\]
where \(\pi\) is a nonnegative measure and \(R\) is a nonnegative continuous linear functional supported at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the product of locally compact, sigma-compact Polish spaces, every nonnegative linear form on the bounded continuous functions decomposes into a nonnegative measure and a nonnegative continuous functional supported at infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kantorovich Duality, Optimality Characterizations, and Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States dual equality under a lower integrable bound, characterizes optimal plans for finite real-valued costs, and gives primal-dual attainment under an additional upper integrable bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal X,\mu)\) and \((\mathcal Y,
u)\) be Polish probability spaces. Let \(c:\mathcal X	imes\mathcal Y	o\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be lower semicontinuous and satisfy \(c(x,y)\geq a(x)+b(y)\), where \(a\in L^1(\mu)\) and \(b\in L^1(
u)\) are real-valued and upper semicontinuous. Then \[\min_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,
u)}\int c\,d\pi=\sup_{\substack{(\psi,\phi)\in C_b(\mathcal X)	imes C_b(\mathcal Y)\ \phi(y)-\psi(x)\leq c(x,y)}}\left(\int\phi\,d
u-\int\psi\,d\muight)\] \[=\sup_{\substack{(\psi,\phi)\in L^1(\mu)	imes L^1(
u)\ \phi(y)-\psi(x)\leq c(x,y)}}\left(\int\phi\,d
u-\int\psi\,d\muight)=\sup_{\psi\in L^1(\mu)}\left(\int\psi^c\,d
u-\int\psi\,d\muight)\] \[=\sup_{\phi\in L^1(
u)}\left(\int\phi\,d
u-\int\phi^c\,d\muight),\] and the suprema may be restricted to c-convex \(\psi\) and c-concave \(\phi\). If \(c\) is real-valued and the optimal cost is finite, there exists a measurable c-cyclically monotone set \(\Gamma\subseteq\mathcal X	imes\mathcal Y\), closed when \(a,b,c\) are continuous, such that for every \(\pi\in\Pi(\mu,
u)\) the following are equivalent: \(\pi\) is optimal; \(\pi\) is c-cyclically monotone; some c-convex \(\psi\) satisfies \(\psi^c(y)-\psi(x)=c(x,y)\) \(\pi\)-almost surely; some \(\psi,\phi\) satisfy \(\phi(y)-\psi(x)\leq c(x,y)\) everywhere with equality \(\pi\)-almost surely; and \(\pi(\Gamma)=1\). If additionally \[c(x,y)\leq c_{\mathcal X}(x)+c_{\mathcal Y}(y),\qquad (c_{\mathcal X},c_{\mathcal Y})\in L^1(\mu)	imes L^1(
u),\] then the primal and dual problems attain their optima; the dual potential may be chosen c-convex with \(\phi=\psi^c\). If also \(a,b,c\) are continuous, a closed c-cyclically monotone \(\Gamma\) can be chosen so that, for every \(\pi\in\Pi(\mu,
u)\) and every c-convex \(\psi\in L^1(\mu)\), \[\pi	ext{ is primal-optimal}\iff\pi(\Gamma)=1,\qquad \psi	ext{ is dual-optimal}\iff\Gamma\subseteq\partial_c\psi.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For lower-semicontinuous costs on Polish probability spaces with an integrable separable lower bound, the Kantorovich primal value equals several continuous, integrable, and c-transform dual formulations. For real-valued finite-cost problems, plan optimality is equivalent to cyclical monotonicity and complementary equality with suitable potentials. An integrable separable upper bound guarantees primal and dual attainment; continuity yields closed-set characterizations.

c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is lower semicontinuous}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: c-Concavity, c-Transform, and c-Superdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dual-side potential calculus corresponding to c-convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) and \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) as in the c-convexity definition, a function \(\phi:\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is \(c\)-concave if \(\phi\not\equiv-\infty\) and \(\phi=\psi^c\) for some \(\psi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\). Its \(c\)-transform and c-superdifferential are \[\phi^c(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}\bigl(\phi(y)-c(x,y)\bigr),\qquad \partial^c\phi=\{(x,y)\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y:\phi(y)-\phi^c(x)=c(x,y)\}.\] The set \(\partial^c\phi\) is \(c\)-cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nontrivial function is c-concave when it is a c-transform. Its reverse c-transform is a supremum of the function minus cost, and equality defines a c-superdifferential whose graph is c-cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi\text{ is }c\text{-concave}\iff \exists\psi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\text{ with }\phi=\psi^c;\quad \phi^c(x)=\sup_y(\phi(y)-c(x,y));\quad \partial^c\phi=\{(x,y):\phi(y)-\phi^c(x)=c(x,y)\}\text{ is }c\text{-cyclically monotone}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for extended-real functions on the two transport spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For u:X\to\overline{\mathbb R},\quad u^c(y):=\inf_{x\in X}\{c(x,y)-u(x)\};\qquad v^c(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}\{c(x,y)-v(y)\}\quad(v:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal cost transforms for the dual constraint \(f(x)+g(y)\le c(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), its cost transform on \(Y\) is
\[
f^c(y):=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(c(x,y)-f(x)\bigr).
\]
For \(g:Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), define analogously
\[
g^c(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}\bigl(c(x,y)-g(y)\bigr).
\]
Whenever these expressions are defined, \(f(x)+f^c(y)\le c(x,y)\) and \(g^c(x)+g(y)\le c(x,y)\). Moreover, \(f_1\le f_2\) implies \(f_1^c\ge f_2^c\), and the analogous order reversal holds for functions on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost transform takes the infimum of cost minus potential over the opposite space; it produces a dual-feasible partner and reverses order.

knowledge_statements.title: Double-Transform Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure identities for the infimal cost-transform convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty sets, and suppose all indicated cost transforms are well-defined. For every admissible \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), \[f\le f^{cc},\qquad f^{ccc}=f^c,\qquad f^{cccc}=f^{cc}.\] Consequently, \(f\mapsto f^{cc}\) is extensive, monotone, and idempotent. Its fixed points are exactly the \(c\)-concave functions on \(X\): \[f\text{ is \(c\)-concave}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^{cc}=f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double cost transformation is an extensive, monotone, idempotent closure whose fixed points are exactly the cost-concave functions.
assumptions_latex: All displayed cost transforms are well-defined and avoid indeterminate extended-real differences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{cc}\ge f\), \(f^{ccc}=f^c\), and \(f\) is \(c\)-concave exactly when \(f^{cc}=f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Points where an extended-valued cost transform ceases to be a finite dual potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the finite transform domain by
\[
D_c(f):=\left\{y\in Y:-\infty<\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(c(x,y)-f(x)\bigr)<+\infty\right\}.
\]
If \(c(x,y)=+\infty\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(f^c(y)=+\infty\). If there exists a sequence \((x_n)\) with \(c(x_n,y)-f(x_n)\to-\infty\), then \(f^c(y)=-\infty\). Therefore the transform is a finite-valued dual potential on a prescribed set \(D\subseteq Y\) only if \(D\subseteq D_c(f)\); outside this boundary the ordinary finite-potential calculus fails.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a dual pair \((\phi,\psi)\), a normalization chooses \(a\in\mathbb R\) and replaces the pair by \((\widehat\phi,\widehat\psi)=(\phi+a,\psi-a)\). Mean normalization imposes
\[
\int_X\widehat\phi\,d\mu=0,
\quad\text{so that}\quad
 a=-\int_X\phi\,d\mu.
\]
If a base point \(x_0\in X\) satisfies \(\phi(x_0)\in\mathbb R\), point normalization imposes \(\widehat\phi(x_0)=0\) and uses \(a=-\phi(x_0)\). If \(\sup_X\phi\in\mathbb R\), supremum normalization imposes \(\sup_X\widehat\phi=0\) and uses \(a=-\sup_X\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mean, point, or supremum condition fixes the additive constant whenever the corresponding integral, point value, or supremum is finite.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-parameter additive symmetry of two-potential Kantorovich duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(a\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
T_a(\phi,\psi):=(\phi+a,\psi-a).
\]
Then \(T_0\) is the identity, \(T_a\circ T_b=T_{a+b}\), and
\[
(\phi(x)+a)+(\psi(y)-a)=\phi(x)+\psi(y)
\]
for all \((x,y)\) where the sums are defined. Consequently, dual feasibility is constant along
\[
\mathcal O(\phi,\psi):=
\{T_a(\phi,\psi):a\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
If both potentials take at least one finite value, the action is free: \(T_a(\phi,\psi)=(\phi,\psi)\) implies \(a=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a constant to one dual potential and subtracting it from the other preserves their sum and hence dual feasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multimarginal optimal-transport dual problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dual problem and distinguishes strong duality from dual attainment; the admissible function class affects the applicable results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For marginals \(\mu_k\) on spaces \(X_k\) and cost \(c:X_1\times\cdots\times X_N\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), the multimarginal dual problem is
\[
\sup_{(\varphi_k)_{k=1}^N}\left\{\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{X_k}\varphi_k\,d\mu_k:\ \sum_{k=1}^N\varphi_k(x_k)\le c(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\ \text{for all }(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\right\}.
\]
Admissible potentials may be chosen from classes such as \(L^1(\mu_k)\), \(C_0(X_k)\), or \(C_b(X_k)\), subject to the hypotheses of the relevant duality theorem. Equality of primal and dual values is strong duality; attainment of the supremum is dual attainment, and attaining functions are optimal potentials. Dual attainment generally requires additional assumptions, with compact \(X_k\) and Lipschitz \(c\) furnishing one standard regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multimarginal dual maximizes the sum of the marginal integrals of potentials whose pointwise sum does not exceed the transport cost. Strong duality means equality of primal and dual values, whereas dual attainment means that admissible optimal potentials exist. Function spaces such as L1, C0, and bounded continuous functions serve in different duality formulations, and attainment generally needs additional compactness or cost regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{(\varphi_k)}\left\{\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{X_k}\varphi_k\,d\mu_k:\sum_{k=1}^N\varphi_k(x_k)\le c(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_0\) be the set of integrable pairs \((\varphi,\psi)\) satisfying \(\varphi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)\), with one additive normalization imposed.
