knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Slope as the Minimum Norm of a Plan Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the Wasserstein metric slope with the minimum plan-subdifferential norm and gives its minimizing-movement approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty] be regular and satisfy (10.3.1a,b), with q=p'. Then \mu\in D(|\partial\phi|) if and only if \boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu)\neq\varnothing, and \[|\partial\phi|(\mu)=\min\{|\gamma|_{2,q}:\gamma\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu)\},\qquad D(|\partial\phi|)=D(\boldsymbol\partial\phi).\] For \mu\in D(|\partial\phi|), if \mu_\tau minimizes (10.3.1b) and \gamma_\tau is the associated rescaled plan, there is a sequence \tau_n\downarrow0 such that \[|\partial\phi|^q(\mu)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{W_p^p(\mu,\mu_{\tau_n})}{p\tau_n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\phi(\mu)-\phi(\mu_{\tau_n})}{\tau_n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}|\gamma_{\tau_n}|_{2,q}^q.\] Every limit point of \gamma_{\tau_n} minimizes the norm formula and is also a limit point in \mathcal P_{pq}(X\times X). When p=2, the same conclusion holds for the strong-subdifferential sequence specified in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a regular functional, finite metric slope is equivalent to existence of a plan subdifferential, and the slope equals its minimum norm. Along a suitable vanishing sequence of minimizing-movement steps, transport displacement, energy decay, and plan-subdifferential norms converge to the slope power, and plan limits attain the minimum.
assumptions_latex: \mu\in D(|\partial\phi|)\text{ for the minimizing-movement approximation clause}
\gamma_\tau\text{ is the associated rescaled plan of Lemma 10.3.4}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(|\partial\phi|)=D(\boldsymbol\partial\phi),\quad |\partial\phi|(\mu)=\min_{\gamma\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu)}|\gamma|_{2,q},\quad\text{with the stated minimizing-movement limits and minimum-norm limit plans.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent Minimizers Generate Strong Plan Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a strong Wasserstein plan subdifferential from an optimal plan joining a minimizing-movement step to its reference measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty] satisfy (10.3.1a), let \mu_\tau minimize (10.3.1b), and let \widehat\gamma_\tau\in\Gamma_o(\mu_\tau,\mu). Define \rho_\tau(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,j_p((x_2-x_1)/\tau)) and \gamma_\tau=(\rho_\tau)_\#\widehat\gamma_\tau. The associated compatible plans \boldsymbol\mu_\tau\in\Gamma(\gamma_\tau,\mu^3) satisfy \[\phi(\mu^3)-\phi(\mu_\tau)-\int_{X^3}\langle x_2,x_3-x_1\rangle\,d\boldsymbol\mu_\tau\geq o(W_{p,\boldsymbol\mu_\tau}(\mu^3,\mu_\tau)).\] Consequently, \gamma_\tau\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu_\tau), and \gamma_\tau is a strong subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling an optimal plan from a minimizing-movement minimizer to its reference measure through the duality map produces a strong plan subdifferential at the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_\tau=(\rho_\tau)_\#\widehat\gamma_\tau\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu_\tau)\quad\text{and}\quad\gamma_\tau\text{ is a strong subdifferential.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization and Lambda-Monotonicity of Plan Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes plan subdifferentials of proper lower-semicontinuous lambda-convex Wasserstein functionals and gives their lambda-monotonicity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \lambda-convex. A plan \gamma\in\mathcal P_{pq}(X\times X) belongs to \boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu^1) if and only if \pi^1_\#\gamma=\mu^1 and, for every \mu^3\in\mathcal P_p(X), there exists \boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\gamma,\mu^3) such that \[\phi(\mu^3)-\phi(\mu^1)\geq\int_{X^3}\langle x_2,x_3-x_1\rangle\,d\boldsymbol\mu+\frac{\lambda}{2}W_p^2(\mu^1,\mu^3).\] This inequality holds for every such optimal plan along which \phi is \lambda-convex. Moreover, if \gamma^i\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu^i) for i=1,2, there exists \boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma(\gamma^1,\gamma^2) with \pi^{1,3}_\#\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\mu^1,\mu^2) and \[\int_{X^4}\langle x_2-x_4,x_1-x_3\rangle\,d\boldsymbol\mu\geq\lambda W_p^2(\mu^1,\mu^2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous lambda-convex functional, plan-subdifferential membership is equivalent to a global supporting inequality along a compatible optimal transport plan. Pairs of plan subdifferentials satisfy a corresponding lambda-monotonicity inequality.
assumptions_latex: \phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and lower semicontinuous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu^1)\iff\text{the stated marginal and global variational inequalities hold, and pairs of plan subdifferentials satisfy the }\lambda\text{-monotonicity bound.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines extended and strong Fréchet subdifferentials represented by transport plans in Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let q=p'=p/(p-1), let \phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty] satisfy (10.3.1a), and let \mu^1\in D(\phi). A plan \gamma\in\mathcal P_{pq}(X\times X) belongs to \boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu^1) if \pi^1_\#\gamma=\mu^1 and, as \mu^3\to\mu^1, \[\phi(\mu^3)-\phi(\mu^1)\geq\inf_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\gamma,\mu^3)}\int_{X^3}\langle x_2,x_3-x_1\rangle\,d\boldsymbol\mu+o(W_p(\mu^1,\mu^3)).\] It is a strong Fréchet subdifferential if, for every compatible plan \boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma(\gamma,\mu^3), \[\phi(\mu^3)-\phi(\mu^1)\geq\int_{X^3}\langle x_2,x_3-x_1\rangle\,d\boldsymbol\mu+o(W_{p,\boldsymbol\mu}(\mu^1,\mu^3)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport plan with first marginal μ¹ is an extended Fréchet plan subgradient when it gives the stated first-order lower estimate after optimization over compatible optimal plans. It is strong when the estimate holds for every compatible plan with the plan-dependent transport distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu^1)\text{ exactly under the marginal and asymptotic inequality conditions, with strong membership under the universal compatible-plan inequality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal Subdifferential of the Opposite Squared Wasserstein Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the metric slope and strong minimal subdifferential through optimal plans and barycentric projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\psi(\mu)=-\frac12W_2^2(\mu,\mu^2)\). Then, for every \(\mu\in\mathcal P_2(X)\), \[|\partial\psi|^2(\mu)=\min\left\{\int_X|\bar\gamma-\mathbf i|^2\,d\mu:\gamma\in\Gamma_o(\mu,\mu^2)\right\}.\] If \(\gamma\) is the unique minimizing plan, then \(\partial^\circ\psi(\mu)=\bar\gamma-\mathbf i\), and this is a strong subdifferential. Moreover, \(\mu\mapsto|\partial\psi|(\mu)\) is lower semicontinuous for narrow convergence along sequences bounded in \(\mathcal P_2(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared slope of the negative half squared Wasserstein distance equals the minimum squared norm of the barycentric displacement over optimal plans. The unique minimizing plan yields a strong minimal subdifferential, and the slope is narrowly lower semicontinuous along P2-bounded sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\partial\psi|^2(\mu)=\min_{\gamma\in\Gamma_o(\mu,\mu^2)}\int_X|\bar\gamma-\mathbf i|^2\,d\mu;\quad \partial^\circ\psi(\mu)=\bar\gamma-\mathbf i\text{ for the unique minimizing plan};\quad |\partial\psi|\text{ is narrowly lower semicontinuous along }\mathcal P_2\text{-bounded sequences}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Functionals in Wasserstein Subdifferential Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines regularity through sequential closedness of strong plan subdifferentials together with identification of the limiting functional value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A functional \phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty] satisfying (10.3.1a) is regular if the following implication holds: whenever strong subdifferentials \gamma_n\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu_n) satisfy \varphi_n=\phi(\mu_n)\to\varphi\in\mathbb R, \mu_n\to\mu in \mathcal P_p(X), \sup_n|\gamma_n|_{2,q}<+\infty, and \gamma_n\to\gamma in \mathcal P(X\times X_\varpi), then \gamma\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu) and \varphi=\phi(\mu).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Wasserstein functional is regular when bounded convergent sequences of its strong plan subdifferentials have a limiting plan subdifferential and convergence of the functional values identifies the value at the limiting measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma\in\boldsymbol\partial\phi(\mu)\quad\text{and}\quad\varphi=\phi(\mu).

children.title: Subdifferential Inclusion Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Relations and separations among strong, extended, and plan formulations.

assumptions_latex: The strong, extended, and plan subdifferentials use the conventions stated in the preceding records.
\(J_\mu(\xi):=(\mathrm{id},\xi)_\#\mu\) embeds a vector field as a deterministic position-velocity plan.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_\mu(\partial_{\rm s}\mathcal E(\mu))\subseteq J_\mu(\partial\mathcal E(\mu))\subseteq\boldsymbol\partial\mathcal E(\mu)\).

notation.meaning: Embedding of a vector field into a deterministic plan

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hierarchy under the coupling-uniform, optimal-plan, and plan-valued conventions above.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\mu\in D(\mathcal E)\), restriction of the strong support inequality to optimal couplings yields
\[
\partial_{\rm s}\mathcal E(\mu)\subseteq\partial\mathcal E(\mu).
\]
Moreover, deterministic lifting preserves the optimal-plan pairing, so
\[
J_\mu\bigl(\partial\mathcal E(\mu)\bigr)
\subseteq\boldsymbol\partial\mathcal E(\mu).
\]
Consequently,
\[
J_\mu\bigl(\partial_{\rm s}\mathcal E(\mu)\bigr)
\subseteq J_\mu\bigl(\partial\mathcal E(\mu)\bigr)
\subseteq\boldsymbol\partial\mathcal E(\mu).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong vector subgradients are extended subgradients, and deterministic lifting turns extended vector subgradients into plan subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Inclusion Hierarchy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the inclusion-hierarchy container, but both inclusions depend on the preceding unverified conventions. A source explicitly supporting these definitions and deterministic lifting is required.

assumptions_latex: For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), \(\mu_\varepsilon=(\mathrm{id}+\varepsilon\zeta)_\#\mu\) lies in the domain of \(\mathcal E\).
\(\xi\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\) supplies a first-order expansion of \(\mathcal E\) at \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\mathcal E(\mu_\varepsilon)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle\,d\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The first variation of \(\mathcal E\) at \(\mu\) is represented by \(\xi\) along transport perturbations if, for every admissible \(\zeta\),
\[
\mathcal E\bigl((\mathrm{id}+\varepsilon\zeta)_\#\mu\bigr)
=\mathcal E(\mu)+\varepsilon
\int_{\mathbb R^d}\langle\xi(x),\zeta(x)\rangle\,d\mu(x)
+o(|\varepsilon|)
\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\to0.
\]
Equivalently, the directional derivative exists and equals the \(L^2(\mu)\) pairing of \(\xi\) with \(\zeta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport first variation differentiates the energy after pushing the measure by the identity plus a small vector field.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barycentric Projection of a Plan
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through disintegration with respect to the first marginal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space and $\gamma\in\mathcal P(X\times X)$. Suppose $\gamma$ admits the disintegration $\gamma=\int_X\gamma_{x_1}\,d\mu(x_1)$ with respect to its first marginal $\mu=(\pi^1)_\#\gamma$, and suppose $\gamma_{x_1}$ has finite first moment for $\mu$-a.e. $x_1$. The barycentric projection of $\gamma$ is the map $\bar\gamma:X\to X$ defined by $\bar\gamma(x_1)=\int_Xx_2\,d\gamma_{x_1}(x_2)$ for $\mu$-a.e. $x_1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disintegrate a plan with respect to its first marginal. When almost every conditional measure has a finite first moment, the barycentric projection assigns to each first coordinate the barycenter of its conditional measure.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a separable Hilbert space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar\gamma(x_1):=\int_Xx_2\,d\gamma_{x_1}(x_2)\quad\text{for }\mu\text{-a.e. }x_1.

children.top_down_role: Breakdown of slope finiteness, relaxation, or lower-semicontinuity.

assumptions_latex:
The descending metric slope is \(|\partial\mathcal E|(\mu)=\limsup_{
u	o\mu}(\mathcal E(\mu)-\mathcal E(
u))^+/W_2(\mu,
u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\partial\mathcal E|(\bar\mu)=+\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct Dirac-family computation exhibits blow-up when local Lipschitz regularity is removed
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete blow-up caused by sublinear radial energy near a Dirac mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(v\neq0\), set \(\nu_t=\delta_{tv}\) with \(t>0\). Then
\[
W_2(\bar\mu,\nu_t)=t|v|,
\qquad
\frac{(\mathcal E(\bar\mu)-\mathcal E(\nu_t))^+}{W_2(\bar\mu,\nu_t)}
=(t|v|)^{-1/2}.
\]
Hence this quotient diverges as \(t\downarrow0\), and therefore
\[
|\partial\mathcal E|(\bar\mu)=+\infty.
\]
Thus finiteness of the metric slope can fail when the energy is not locally Lipschitz at the base measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square-root cusp of Wasserstein distance has infinite descending slope at its central Dirac mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Slope Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterphenomenon is mathematically plausible and failure_boundary is the correct role, but it has no citation and the statement includes a computation serving as proof text. A sourced, proof-free candidate is required.

children.title: Subdifferential Failures
children.top_down_role: Absence or instability of suitable Wasserstein subdifferential objects.

assumptions_latex: Use the optimal-plan vector-field subdifferential at \(\bar\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\partial\mathcal E|(\bar\mu)=1\) but \(\partial\mathcal E(\bar\mu)=\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the Dirac embedding reduces the claim to the nonsubdifferentiability of minus the Euclidean norm
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite slope without a supporting Wasserstein subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Along \(\nu_t=\delta_{tv}\), one has \(W_2(\bar\mu,\nu_t)=t|v|\) and \(\mathcal E(\nu_t)=-t|v|\), which gives \(|\partial\mathcal E|(\bar\mu)=1\). If \(\xi\in L^2(\bar\mu;\mathbb R^d)\) were a subgradient, writing \(a=\xi(0)\) would require
\[
-|v|\geq\langle a,v\rangle
\quad\text{for every }v\in\mathbb R^d.
\]
Applying the inequality to \(v\) and \(-v\) is impossible for \(v\neq0\). Thus \(\partial\mathcal E(\bar\mu)=\varnothing\), despite the finite slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minus the distance to a Dirac mass has finite slope there but admits no linear Wasserstein subgradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example fits the Subdifferential Failures leaf and counterexample is the correct kind, but it depends on the unverified optimal-plan subdifferential convention, has no citation, and includes proof text.

children.title: Chain-Rule Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of valid energy differentiation along admissible measure curves.

assumptions_latex: Let \(\mathcal E(\mu)=0\) if \(\mu=\delta_0\) and \(\mathcal E(\mu)=1\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\partial\mathcal E|(\mu_t)=0\) for every \(t\), but \(t\mapsto\mathcal E(\mu_t)\) is not absolutely continuous.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: an isolated energy well shows that the local slope need not be a strong upper gradient
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the slope chain rule without an upper-gradient hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curve satisfies \(W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)=|s-t|\), hence it is absolutely continuous with metric speed one. The energy is locally constant near every \(\delta_t\) with \(t\neq0\), while no nearby measure has energy below \(\mathcal E(\delta_0)=0\); therefore
\[
|\partial\mathcal E|(\mu_t)=0
\quad\text{for all }t.
\]
Nevertheless, \(\mathcal E(\mu_t)=1\) for \(t\neq0\) and \(\mathcal E(\mu_0)=0\), so the composition is not absolutely continuous. Thus the metric slope alone does not guarantee a chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isolated energy well has zero descending slope everywhere along a Dirac curve, yet the composed energy jumps.
knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Rule Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The isolated-well example correctly targets failure of a slope-based chain rule, but no source identifies the applicable chain-rule or upper-gradient framework, and the statement contains proof text.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete action bound for Fokker–Planck minimizing movements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform squared-Wasserstein increment estimate controlled by the initial free-energy gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau>0\), and let \((\rho_k^\tau)_{k\ge0}\) be the Fokker\text{--}Planck JKO sequence. If \(J(\rho_0)<+\infty\) and \(\inf_{\mathcal P(\Omega)}J> -\infty\), then \[\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{W_2^2(\rho_{k+1}^\tau,\rho_k^\tau)}{\tau}\le 2\left(J(\rho_0)-\inf_{\mathcal P(\Omega)}J\right).\]

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space, \(T>0\), and \(\mathcal E:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(g:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a strong upper gradient for \(\mathcal E\).
\(u:[0,T]\to X\) is locally absolutely continuous and \(\mathcal E(u(0))<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is a curve of maximal slope for \(\mathcal E\) with respect to \(g\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard quadratic energy-dissipation definition of a curve of maximal slope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic curves of maximal slope in a complete metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curve \(u\) is a curve of maximal slope for \(\mathcal E\) with respect to \(g\) if \(t\mapsto\mathcal E(u(t))\) agrees almost everywhere with a nonincreasing function and, for every \(0\leq s\leq t\leq T\),
\[
\mathcal E(u(t))+\frac{1}{2}\int_s^t|u'|^2(r)\,dr
+\frac{1}{2}\int_s^t g^2(u(r))\,dr
\leq\mathcal E(u(s)).
\]
Here \(|u'|\) denotes the metric derivative, defined for almost every time along an absolutely continuous curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curve of maximal slope dissipates energy at least as fast as half its squared speed plus half the squared upper gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Curves of Maximal Slope

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of Wasserstein gradient flows and curves of maximal slope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes gradient flows of regular functionals on \(\mathcal P_p(X)\) and identifies their minimal tangent field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be regular and satisfy conditions \((11.1.13a,b)\). A curve \(\mu:(0,\infty)\to\mathcal P_p(X)\) is a \(p\)-curve of maximal slope with respect to \(|\partial\phi|\) if and only if it is a gradient flow and \(t\mapsto\phi(\mu_t)\) agrees \(\mathcal L^1\)-a.e. with a function of bounded variation. In that case its tangent field satisfies \(v_t=-\partial^\circ\phi(\mu_t)\) for \(\mathcal L^1\)-a.e. \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a regular functional satisfying the stated structural conditions, a Wasserstein curve is a p-curve of maximal slope exactly when it is a gradient flow and its energy has a bounded-variation representative. Its tangent velocity is then the negative minimal subdifferential selection almost everywhere.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and regularity of Wasserstein gradient flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subsequential construction by the variational scheme, with stronger dissipation and pointwise conclusions under geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and satisfy the weak lower-semicontinuity and bounded-slope continuity condition. For every \(\mu_0\in D(\phi)\), each sequence of discrete solutions \(\bar M_{\tau_k}\) of the variational scheme admits a subsequence converging narrowly in \(\mathcal P(X_\varpi)\), locally uniformly on \([0,+\infty)\), to \(\mu\in AC^p_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,+\infty);\mathcal P_p(X))\). Its tangent vector satisfies \(j_p(v_t)=-\partial^\circ\phi(\mu_t)\) and \(\|v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t;X)}=|\mu'|(t)\) for \(\mathcal L^1\)-a.e. \(t>0\), while \(\mu_t\to\mu_0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). There is an \(\mathcal L^1\)-negligible set \(\mathcal N\subset(0,+\infty)\) such that \(\int_a^b\int_X|v_t(x)|^p\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt+\phi(\mu_b)\leq\phi(\mu_a)\) whenever \(b\geq0\) and \(a\in[0,b)\setminus\mathcal N\). If \(\phi\) is also \(\lambda\)-convex along geodesics, this is an equality for every \(0\leq a<b<+\infty\); the curve is locally Lipschitz on \((0,+\infty)\), and on \([0,+\infty)\) when \(\mu_0\in D(|\partial\phi|)\); \(\mu_t\in D(\partial\phi)\) for every \(t>0\); and \(t\mapsto e^{\lambda t}|\partial\phi|(\mu_t)\) is right-continuous. For each \(t>0\) and choices \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{t,h}\in\Gamma_o(\mu_t,\mu_{t+h})\), the right limit \(\boldsymbol\mu_{t,0}=\lim_{h\downarrow0}(\pi^1,j_p((\pi^1-\pi^2)/h))_\#\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{t,h}\) exists in \(\mathcal P_{pq}(X\times X)\), equals \(\partial^\circ\phi(\mu_t)\), and satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt_+}\phi(\mu_t)=-\int_{X^2}|x_2|^q\,d\boldsymbol\mu_{t,0}=-|\partial\phi|^q(\mu_t)=-|\mu'|^p(t)\). These right-limit identities hold at \(t=0\) if and only if \(\mu_0\in D(\partial\phi)=D(|\partial\phi|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete variational solutions have a subsequence converging locally uniformly in the narrow topology to an absolutely continuous Wasserstein gradient flow. The limit satisfies the tangent-vector equation, the initial condition, and an energy inequality outside a negligible set of starting times. Under geodesic lambda-convexity, it satisfies an energy identity, regularizes, and admits right-limit representations of the minimal subdifferential and pointwise energy dissipation. Those pointwise identities extend to time zero exactly for initial data in the subdifferential domain.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\mathcal P_p(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\phi\) satisfies the weak lower-semicontinuity and bounded-slope continuity condition of Assumption 11.3.1.
\(\mu_0\in D(\phi)\), and \(\bar M_{\tau_k}\) is a sequence of discrete solutions of the variational scheme.
The strengthened conclusions assume that \(\phi\) is \(\lambda\)-convex along geodesics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subsequence converges to an \(AC^p_{\mathrm{loc}}\) Wasserstein gradient flow satisfying the gradient-flow equation and energy inequality; geodesic \(\lambda\)-convexity yields the stated energy identity, regularization, right-limit subdifferential representation, and pointwise dissipation identities.

\(u:[0,T]\to X\) is absolutely continuous and \(g:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a strong upper gradient for \(\mathcal E\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic EDI and EDE under a strong upper-gradient chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(0\leq s\leq t\leq T\), the energy-dissipation inequality
\[
\mathcal E(u(t))+\frac{1}{2}\int_s^t|u'|^2(r)\,dr+\frac{1}{2}\int_s^t g^2(u(r))\,dr\leq\mathcal E(u(s))
\]
holds if and only if
\[
\mathcal E(u(t))+\frac{1}{2}\int_s^t|u'|^2(r)\,dr+\frac{1}{2}\int_s^t g^2(u(r))\,dr=\mathcal E(u(s)),
\]
and \(|u'|(r)=g(u(r))\) for almost every \(r\in(s,t)\). The equality is the quadratic energy-dissipation equality formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a valid strong-upper-gradient chain rule, the energy-dissipation inequality is equivalent to the energy-dissipation equality, and the metric speed equals the upper gradient almost everywhere.

notation.meaning: Evolution variational inequality with convexity parameter lambda

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exponential contraction is the standard comparison consequence of two EVI inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contraction for two solutions of the same autonomous \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume that for every \(w\in D(\mathcal E)\), both curves satisfy, for almost every \(t>0\),
\[
\frac12\frac{d}{dt}d^2(u(t),w)+\frac\lambda2d^2(u(t),w)
\leq\mathcal E(w)-\mathcal E(u(t)),
\]
with the analogous inequality for \(v\). Then their distance obeys
\[
d(u(t),v(t))\leq e^{-\lambda(t-s)}d(u(s),v(s))
\quad\text{for all }0\leq s\leq t\leq T.
\]
In particular, taking \(s=0\) gives exponential flow contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two solutions of the same lambda-EVI contract exponentially, with rate lambda, relative to their initial distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow Contraction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and exponential contraction conclusion fit the Flow Contraction leaf, but an authoritative EVI theorem with the required curve regularity and comparison hypotheses is not cited.

children.title: Flow Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Uniqueness of gradient-flow trajectories selected by the EVI structure.

assumptions_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) are \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\) solutions for the same energy on \([0,T]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u(t)=v(t)\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\).

notation.meaning: Evolution variational inequality with parameter lambda

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniqueness follows immediately from EVI contraction at zero initial distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness within the class of solutions satisfying the same EVI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The contraction estimate for two \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\) solutions gives
\[
d(u(t),v(t))\leq e^{-\lambda t}d(u(0),v(0))
\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T].
\]
If \(u(0)=v(0)\), the right-hand side is zero. Hence \(d(u(t),v(t))=0\) for every \(t\), and therefore \(u(t)=v(t)\) throughout \([0,T]\). Thus at most one \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\) flow trajectory starts from any prescribed initial datum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EVI contraction forces any two EVI trajectories with the same initial measure to coincide at every later time.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow Uniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniqueness theorem fits the terminal container and follows formally from the stated contraction estimate, but that prerequisite estimate and its EVI hypotheses have no inspectable authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform additive perturbations of two EVI energies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(t)=d^2(S_t^E x,S_t^F y)\). Then \(q'(t)+2\lambda q(t)\le4\varepsilon\) for almost every \(t>0\). Consequently, if \(\lambda\ne0\), then \(q(t)\le e^{-2\lambda t}q(0)+\frac{2\varepsilon}{\lambda}(1-e^{-2\lambda t})\); if \(\lambda=0\), then \(q(t)\le q(0)+4\varepsilon t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform energy discrepancy at the states visited by two EVI flows gives an explicit bound on their squared distance.

For every \(t\ge0\), both \(|E(S_t^E x)-F(S_t^E x)|\le\varepsilon\) and \(|E(S_t^F y)-F(S_t^F y)|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(q(t):=d^2(S_t^E x,S_t^F y)\), one has \(q'(t)+2\lambda q(t)\le4\varepsilon\) almost everywhere, with the stated integrated bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^{E_n}\) and \(S^E\) denote the associated EVI semigroups. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interpolation of Kantorovich dual potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint conjugate potentials propagated by Hamilton–Jacobi evolution remain dual-optimal between every pair of intermediate measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\), \((\mathcal A)^{0,1}\), and \(c^{s,t}\) be as in the Hamilton–Jacobi cost-transform setting. Let \(\mu_0,\mu_1\) be probability measures with \(C^{0,1}(\mu_0,\mu_1)<+\infty\), and let \((\psi_0,\phi_1)\) be \(c^{0,1}\)-conjugate such that every optimal plan from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu_1\) is supported in \(\partial_{c^{0,1}}\psi_0\). If \((\mu_r)_{0\le r\le1}\) is a displacement interpolation and \(s<t\), set \(\psi_s=H_+^{0,s}\psi_0\) and \(\phi_t=H_-^{1,t}\phi_1\). Then \((\psi_s,\phi_t)\) is optimal for the Kantorovich dual problem between \(\mu_s\) and \(\mu_t\) with cost \(c^{s,t}\), \[C^{s,t}(\mu_s,\mu_t)=\int\phi_t\,d\mu_t-\int\psi_s\,d\mu_s.\] Moreover, \(\phi_t(y)-\psi_s(x)\le c^{s,t}(x,y)\), with equality \(\pi_{s,t}\)-almost surely for every optimal plan \(\pi_{s,t}\) between \(\mu_s\) and \(\mu_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If endpoint Kantorovich potentials are cost-conjugate and every endpoint optimal plan is supported on the corresponding cost-subdifferential, then propagating the potentials by the forward and backward Hamilton–Jacobi transforms yields an optimal dual pair between any two intermediate measures of a displacement interpolation. The intermediate transport cost equals the dual value, and the dual constraint is saturated almost surely under every intermediate optimal plan.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) carries a coercive Lagrangian action with costs \(c^{s,t}\).
Every optimal plan \(\pi_{0,1}\) between \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\) satisfies \(\operatorname{supp}\pi_{0,1}\subseteq\partial_{c^{0,1}}\psi_0\).
\((\mu_r)_{0\le r\le1}\) is a displacement interpolation between \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\psi_s,\phi_t)\text{ is dual-optimal for }(\mu_s,\mu_t,c^{s,t});\quad C^{s,t}(\mu_s,\mu_t)=\int\phi_t\,d\mu_t-\int\psi_s\,d\mu_s;\quad \phi_t(y)-\psi_s(x)\le c^{s,t}(x,y),\text{ with equality }\pi_{s,t}\text{-a.s. for every optimal }\pi_{s,t}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order, composition, and adjunction properties of Hamilton–Jacobi semigroups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary algebraic properties of the forward and backward cost transforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Hamilton–Jacobi operators induced by a coercive Lagrangian action: (i) every admissibly indexed \(H_+\) and \(H_-\) is order-preserving; (ii) for \(t_1<t_2<t_3\), \[H_+^{t_2,t_3}H_+^{t_1,t_2}=H_+^{t_1,t_3},\qquad H_-^{t_2,t_1}H_-^{t_3,t_2}=H_-^{t_3,t_1};\] and (iii) for \(s<t\), pointwise, \[H_-^{t,s}H_+^{s,t}\le\operatorname{Id},\qquad H_+^{s,t}H_-^{t,s}\ge\operatorname{Id}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hamilton–Jacobi cost transforms preserve pointwise order, compose consistently across intermediate times, and satisfy one-sided inverse inequalities: backward-after-forward lies below the identity, while forward-after-backward lies above it.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\), the coercive Lagrangian action, the costs \(c^{s,t}\), and the operators \(H_+^{s,t},H_-^{t,s}\) are as in the cost-transform definition.
\(0\le s<t\le1\) for the one-sided inverse inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi\le\bar\psi\Rightarrow H_\pm\psi\le H_\pm\bar\psi;\quad H_+^{t_2,t_3}H_+^{t_1,t_2}=H_+^{t_1,t_3};\quad H_-^{t_2,t_1}H_-^{t_3,t_2}=H_-^{t_3,t_1};\quad H_-^{t,s}H_+^{s,t}\le\operatorname{Id};\quad H_+^{s,t}H_-^{t,s}\ge\operatorname{Id}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward and backward Hamilton–Jacobi cost transforms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Hopf–Lax/Lax–Oleinik evolution operators and records their general non-invertibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a metric space and \((\mathcal A)^{0,1}\) a coercive Lagrangian action with costs \(c^{s,t}\). For \(0\le s<t\le1\), \(\psi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and \(\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\), define \[H_+^{s,t}\psi(y)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\{\psi(x)+c^{s,t}(x,y)\},\qquad H_-^{t,s}\phi(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal X}\{\phi(y)-c^{s,t}(x,y)\}.\] These are respectively the forward and backward Hamilton–Jacobi, Hopf–Lax, or Lax–Oleinik evolution operators. In general, \(H_-^{t,s}H_+^{s,t}\ne\operatorname{Id}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a coercive Lagrangian action on a metric space, the forward evolution is infimal convolution with the action cost and the backward evolution is the corresponding supremal cost transform. These families are the forward and backward Hamilton–Jacobi–Hopf–Lax–Lax–Oleinik semigroups, but they are not generally mutual inverses.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal A)^{0,1}\) is a coercive Lagrangian action with costs \(c^{s,t}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_+^{s,t}\psi(y)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}(\psi(x)+c^{s,t}(x,y)),\quad H_-^{t,s}\phi(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal X}(\phi(y)-c^{s,t}(x,y)),\quad H_-^{t,s}H_+^{s,t}\ne\operatorname{Id}\text{ in general}.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex EVI Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by loss of geodesic semiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E(\delta_x)=-|x|\) on \(X=\{\delta_x:x\in\mathbb R\}\), the curves \(u_+(t)=\delta_t\) and \(u_-(t)=\delta_{-t}\) are distinct curves of maximal slope starting from \(\delta_0\). Thus maximal-slope evolution is nonunique, whereas an \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) evolution from a fixed initial datum would be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The descending-cusp energy has two maximal-slope flows from the same state, showing that nonconvex maximal-slope dynamics need not have the uniqueness enforced by an EVI.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distinct curves \(u_+(t)=\delta_t\) and \(u_-(t)=\delta_{-t}\) are maximal-slope flows from \(\delta_0\), so maximal-slope evolution is nonunique for this energy.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimizing-Movement Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit-Euler minimizing-movement representation of the JKO scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\rho_\tau^0=\rho^0\) and, for \(k\ge1\), choose \(\rho_\tau^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)}\left\{E(\rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\rho,\rho_\tau^{k-1})\right\}\). With \(\bar\rho_\tau(t)=\rho_\tau^k\) for \(t\in((k-1)\tau,k\tau]\), any locally uniform \(W_2\)-limit of \(\bar\rho_{\tau_j}\) along \(\tau_j\downarrow0\) is a minimizing movement for \(E\) in this topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The JKO recursion is the metric implicit-Euler scheme, and locally uniform Wasserstein limits of its interpolants are minimizing movements.
assumptions_latex: \(E:\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\tau>0\), \(\rho^0\in D(E)\), and every incremental minimization problem has a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The JKO iterates form the implicit-Euler minimizing-movement approximation of \(E\), and any specified locally uniform \(W_2\)-limit is a minimizing movement.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the canonical implicit-Euler minimizing-movement construction in Wasserstein space

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\le s\le t\le T\), the piecewise-constant interpolants satisfy \(W_2(\bar\rho_\tau(t),\bar\rho_\tau(s))\le C_T^{1/2}(|t-s|+\tau)^{1/2}\). Thus they have a uniform one-half-Hölder time modulus up to the mesh error.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial tightness from a uniform second-moment bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(R>0\), \(\sup_{\tau>0}\sup_{0\le t\le T}\bar\rho_\tau(t)(\mathbb R^d\setminus B_R)\le M_T/R^2\). Hence \(\{\bar\rho_\tau(t):\tau>0,\ 0\le t\le T\}\) is uniformly tight. If the second moments are uniformly integrable, narrow relative compactness upgrades to relative compactness in \(W_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform second-moment bound controls mass outside large balls and gives uniform tightness; uniform integrability of the second moments additionally yields Wasserstein relative compactness.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar\rho_\tau(t)\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) and \(\sup_{\tau>0}\sup_{0\le t\le T}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|x|^2\,d\bar\rho_\tau(t)(x)\le M_T<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(R>0\), \(\sup_{\tau>0}\sup_{0\le t\le T}\bar\rho_\tau(t)(\mathbb R^d\setminus B_R)\le M_T/R^2\), so the family is uniformly tight.

children.top_down_role: Characterization of limits obtained from minimizing-movement interpolants.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar\rho_{\tau_j}\to\rho\) locally uniformly in time with respect to \(W_2\), where \(\tau_j\downarrow0\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak flux compactness identifies the limiting continuity equation and metric velocity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of limiting motion through discrete fluxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Passing to the limit in the discrete weak continuity relation gives \(\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0\) in distributions on \((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d\). Lower semicontinuity of the kinetic action gives \(\int_0^T\int|v|^2\,d\rho\,dt\le\liminf_j\int_0^T\int|v_{\tau_j}|^2\,d\bar\rho_{\tau_j}\,dt\). Consequently \(\rho\in AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2)\) and \(|\rho'|(t)\le\|v_t\|_{L^2(\rho_t)}\) for almost every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent discrete densities and fluxes identify a limiting continuity equation and an admissible Wasserstein velocity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Distributional convergence of the flux alone does not imply the limiting continuity equation; an exact or vanishing-error discrete weak continuity relation is also required. The meaning of the product convergence and the discrete interpolation must be specified by a source before the statement can be repaired reliably.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a convex Wasserstein gradient flow from JKO limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The discrete variational inequality for each JKO step passes to the limit under the stated compactness and lower-semicontinuity hypotheses. The limit curve therefore satisfies, for every \(\sigma\in D(E)\), \(\frac12\frac{d}{dt}W_2^2(\rho_t,\sigma)+\frac\lambda2W_2^2(\rho_t,\sigma)\le E(\sigma)-E(\rho_t)\) for almost every \(t>0\). Thus \(\rho\) is the \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) gradient flow of \(E\); EVI contraction makes the limit unique and removes subsequence dependence.

children.title: Inexact JKO Schemes

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact JKO Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive objective-error formulation of an inexact JKO step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,d)\) be a complete separable metric space, let \(\mathcal F:\mathcal P_2(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\rho^0\in\operatorname{dom}\mathcal F\). Given \(\tau_k>0\) and \(\eta_k\ge0\), an inexact JKO sequence chooses, for every \(k\ge1\), a measure \(\rho^k\in\mathcal P_2(X)\) satisfying
\[
\mathcal F(\rho^k)+\frac{W_2^2(\rho^k,\rho^{k-1})}{2\tau_k}
\le
\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(X)}\left\{\mathcal F(\rho)+\frac{W_2^2(\rho,\rho^{k-1})}{2\tau_k}\right\}+\eta_k.
\]
Writing \(t_0=0\) and \(t_k=\sum_{j=1}^k\tau_j\), the scheme produces the piecewise-constant interpolation \(\bar\rho(t)=\rho^k\) for \(t\in(t_{k-1},t_k]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete separable metric space, each time step approximately minimizes the JKO objective within a prescribed nonnegative additive error and produces a piecewise-constant discrete trajectory.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete separable metric space
A measure satisfying the displayed inexact inequality exists at every step
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal J_k(\rho^k)\le\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(X)}\mathcal J_k(\rho)+\eta_k\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures on X with finite second moment
quadratic Wasserstein distance induced by d

children.title: Regularized JKO Schemes
children.top_down_role: Time-discrete schemes modified by auxiliary regularization.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized JKO Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization of a regularized energy within each JKO step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,d)\) be a complete separable metric space, let \(\mathcal F,\mathcal R:\mathcal P_2(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\rho^0\in\mathcal P_2(X)\). Given \(\tau_k>0\) and \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\), the regularized JKO scheme selects, for every \(k\ge1\),
\[
\rho^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(X)}
\left\{\mathcal F(\rho)+\varepsilon_k\mathcal R(\rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau_k}W_2^2(\rho,\rho^{k-1})\right\}.
\]
The coefficient \(\varepsilon_k\) changes the minimized energy and is therefore distinct from an optimization tolerance permitting a nonminimal iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete separable metric space, a regularized JKO step exactly minimizes the original energy plus a weighted auxiliary regularizer and the Wasserstein proximal term.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete separable metric space
Each displayed minimization admits a solution
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(X)}\{\mathcal F(\rho)+\varepsilon_k\mathcal R(\rho)+(2\tau_k)^{-1}W_2^2(\rho,\rho^{k-1})\}\).

notation.meaning: quadratic Wasserstein distance induced by d

children.title: Error–Regularization Balance
children.top_down_role: Scaling regimes coordinating approximation error with regularization strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Error–Regularization Balance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step additive decomposition of optimization and regularization errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,d)\) be a complete separable metric space and define
\[
\mathcal J_k(\rho)=\mathcal F(\rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau_k}W_2^2(\rho,\rho^{k-1})
\quad\text{for }\rho\in\mathcal P_2(X),
\]
where \(\tau_k>0\), \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\), and \(\eta_k\ge0\). Suppose
\[
\mathcal J_k(\rho^k)+\varepsilon_k\mathcal R(\rho^k)
\le\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(X)}\{\mathcal J_k(\rho)+\varepsilon_k\mathcal R(\rho)\}+\eta_k,
\]
let \(\sigma^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(X)}\mathcal J_k(\rho)\), and assume \(\mathcal R(\sigma^k)-\mathcal R(\rho^k)\le B_k\). Then
\[
0\le\mathcal J_k(\rho^k)-\mathcal J_k(\sigma^k)
\le\eta_k+\varepsilon_k\bigl(\mathcal R(\sigma^k)-\mathcal R(\rho^k)\bigr)
\le\eta_k+\varepsilon_kB_k.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unregularized one-step objective gap is bounded by the optimization tolerance plus the nonnegative regularization strength times a bounded regularizer discrepancy.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete separable metric space
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le\mathcal J_k(\rho^k)-\mathcal J_k(\sigma^k)\le\eta_k+\varepsilon_kB_k\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on the regularizer discrepancy

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}\mathcal J_\tau=\{\delta_{-1},\delta_1\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete extended-valued energy exhibiting two discrete JKO minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\mathcal F:\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R)\to[0,+\infty]\) by \(\mathcal F(\delta_{-1})=\mathcal F(\delta_1)=0\) and \(\mathcal F(\rho)=+\infty\) otherwise. From \(\rho^0=\delta_0\), the JKO objective is
\[
\mathcal J_\tau(\rho)=\mathcal F(\rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\rho,\delta_0).
\]
Both admissible measures have value \(1/(2\tau)\), and every other measure has infinite value. Hence the discrete minimizer is not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An energy finite only at two equidistant Dirac measures gives a JKO step with exactly two minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Minimizer Nonuniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The self-contained counterexample is mathematically correct and the content kind fits the nonuniqueness leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Time-Discretization Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of stability, consistency, or compactness in discrete-time approximations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\tau>1\), \(\inf\mathcal J_\tau=-\infty\); for \(\tau=1\), coercivity is lost.

notation.meaning: JKO objective from the initial Dirac mass

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp loss of one-step coercivity for a negative quadratic energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\rho\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\), set \(\mathcal F(\rho)=-\frac12\int|x|^2\,d\rho(x)\). Since \(W_2^2(\rho,\delta_0)=\int|x|^2\,d\rho(x)\),
\[
\mathcal J_\tau(\rho)=\left(\frac{1}{2\tau}-\frac12\right)\int|x|^2\,d\rho(x).
\]
Thus \(\tau<1\) yields the unique minimizer \(\delta_0\), \(\tau=1\) makes every measure a minimizer, and \(\tau>1\) makes the objective unbounded below. The JKO step therefore fails beyond the coercivity threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For negative quadratic energy, the JKO objective loses uniqueness at step size one and becomes unbounded below above one.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Discretization Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold computation is correct and failure_boundary is the appropriate role, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Selection Dependence
children.top_down_role: Dependence of discrete trajectories or limits on choices among minimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent trajectory dependence caused by the first nonunique JKO selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\tau>0\) and define \(\mathcal F:\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R)\to[0,+\infty]\) by \(\mathcal F(\delta_{-1})=\mathcal F(\delta_1)=0\) and \(\mathcal F(\rho)=+\infty\) for every other \(\rho\). Starting from \(\rho^0=\delta_0\), both \(\delta_{-1}\) and \(\delta_1\) minimize the first JKO objective. Selecting \(\rho^1=\delta_{-1}\) yields the unique later selections \(\rho^k=\delta_{-1}\) for every \(k\ge1\), whereas selecting \(\tilde\rho^1=\delta_1\) yields \(\tilde\rho^k=\delta_1\) for every \(k\ge1\). Thus the discrete evolution and its interpolation depend on the minimizer-selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any fixed positive time step, two equally valid first-step minimizers generate distinct persistent JKO trajectories, so the discrete evolution depends on the selection rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho^k=\delta_{-1}\) and \(\tilde\rho^k=\delta_1\) for every \(k\ge1\) are two valid JKO trajectories.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diffusion PDE–SDE Law Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic representation of the stated linear diffusion equation on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold with a $C^2$ metric whose Ricci curvature tensor is uniformly bounded below, and let $\sigma(t,x):T_xM\to T_xM$ be a twice differentiable linear mapping. If $X_t$ solves $dX_t=\sqrt{2}\,\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ for $0\le t<T$, then $\mu_t$ is a weak solution of $\partial_t\mu=\nabla_x\cdot\bigl((\sigma\sigma^*)\nabla_x\mu\bigr)$ on $M\times[0,T)$ if and only if $\mu_t=\operatorname{law}(X_t)$ for every $t\in[0,T)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated manifold and coefficient assumptions, weak solutions of the displayed linear diffusion equation are exactly the time-marginal laws of the associated stochastic differential equation.

\sigma(t,x):T_xM\to T_xM\text{ is a twice differentiable linear mapping}

children.title: Heat Flows
children.top_down_role: Entropy-driven Wasserstein gradient-flow interpretation of linear heat evolution.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t\), with \(\rho_t=G_t*\rho_0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean heat semigroup as the Wasserstein gradient flow of entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \(W_2\)-gradient flow of \(\operatorname{Ent}\) starting from \(\rho_0\) is the heat semigroup:
\[
\rho_t=G_t*\rho_0,
\qquad
\partial_t\rho_t=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho_t\nabla\frac{\delta\operatorname{Ent}}{\delta\rho}(\rho_t)\right)
=\nabla\cdot(\rho_t\nabla\log\rho_t)=\Delta\rho_t.
\]
Equivalently, \(\rho_t\) is obtained as the vanishing-step limit of JKO minimizations for the entropy functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Wasserstein gradient flow of Boltzmann entropy is the heat equation and equals convolution with the heat kernel.
knowledge_statements.title: Heat Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is standard and fits the heat-flow leaf, but the entropy-gradient-flow identification and JKO convergence assertion lack an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Diffusion Flows
children.top_down_role: Gradient-flow structures for broader diffusion energies and mobilities.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{GF}_{W_2}(\kappa\operatorname{Ent})\) satisfies \(\partial_t\rho_t=\kappa\Delta\rho_t\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-coefficient linear diffusion in the standard Euclidean Wasserstein metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mathcal E_\kappa(\rho)=\kappa\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho\log\rho\,dx\), its \(W_2\)-gradient flow obeys
\[
\partial_t\rho_t
=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho_t\nabla\frac{\delta\mathcal E_\kappa}{\delta\rho}(\rho_t)\right)
=\kappa\nabla\cdot(\rho_t\nabla\log\rho_t)
=\kappa\Delta\rho_t.
\]
Consequently \(\rho_t=H_{\kappa t}\rho_0\). The diffusivity rescales the entropy and, equivalently, rescales time in the heat flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling entropy by a positive diffusivity produces the constant-coefficient diffusion equation and rescales heat-flow time.
knowledge_statements.title: Diffusion Flows

children.title: Fokker–Planck Flows
children.top_down_role: Drift-diffusion evolutions generated by entropy plus confinement energy.

assumptions_latex: \(\rho_0\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) has finite free energy
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t+\nabla\cdot(\rho_t\nabla V)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overdamped Fokker–Planck equation with unit diffusion and potential drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \(W_2\)-gradient flow of the free energy
\[
\mathcal F_V(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho\log\rho\,dx+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)\,d\rho(x)
\]
satisfies
\[
\partial_t\rho_t
=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho_t\nabla\frac{\delta\mathcal F_V}{\delta\rho}(\rho_t)\right)
=\nabla\cdot\bigl(\rho_t\nabla(\log\rho_t+V)\bigr)
=\Delta\rho_t+\nabla\cdot(\rho_t\nabla V).
\]
Thus entropy generates diffusion and potential energy generates the drift term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Wasserstein gradient flow of entropy plus potential energy is the Fokker–Planck equation with diffusion and potential drift.
knowledge_statements.title: Fokker–Planck Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formal Fokker–Planck identity is standard, but boundedness below and C^2 regularity alone do not transparently guarantee the asserted Wasserstein gradient flow for an arbitrary potential; a source is needed to specify sufficient growth or semiconvexity hypotheses.

children.title: Porous-Medium Flows
children.top_down_role: Nonlinear diffusion gradient flows in the slow-diffusion regime.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta(\rho_t^m)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard porous-medium equation as an internal-energy Wasserstein gradient flow.

source_refs.locator: VII.3 The Filtration of a Liquid through a Porous Medium p. 227
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m>1\), the first variation of \(\mathcal U_m\) is \(\delta\mathcal U_m/\delta\rho=p_m(\rho)\). Its \(W_2\)-gradient flow therefore satisfies
\[
\partial_t\rho_t
=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho_t\nabla p_m(\rho_t)\right)
=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho_t\nabla\frac{m}{m-1}\rho_t^{m-1}\right)
=\Delta(\rho_t^m).
\]
The mobility degenerates where \(\rho_t=0\), distinguishing porous-medium diffusion from the heat flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For exponent above one, the Wasserstein gradient flow of power internal energy is the porous-medium equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Porous-Medium Flows

source_witnesses.locator: VII.3 The Filtration of a Liquid through a Porous Medium p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula and representation role are standard, but the cited porous-medium section does not by its locator establish the Wasserstein-gradient-flow characterization. A source specifically supporting that identification is required.

children.title: Fast-Diffusion Flows
children.top_down_role: Nonlinear diffusion gradient flows in the fast-diffusion regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Fast-Diffusion Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Displacement-convex fast-diffusion range for probability densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\ge1\) and let \(m\) satisfy \(0<m<1\) and \(m\ge1-1/d\). For
\[
\mathcal U_m(\rho)=\frac{1}{m-1}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho(x)^m\,dx,
\]
the formal first variation generates
\[
\partial_t\rho_t
=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho_t\nabla\frac{m}{m-1}\rho_t^{m-1}\right)
=\Delta(\rho_t^m).
\]
Because \(m-1<0\), the effective diffusivity \(m\rho_t^{m-1}\) grows as \(\rho_t\) approaches zero. In the stated range, \(\mathcal U_m\) is displacement convex on its finite-energy domain, giving the standard Wasserstein gradient-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive exponent below one and at or above the displacement-convexity threshold, power internal energy generates the fast-diffusion equation in the standard Wasserstein formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta(\rho_t^m)\).

children.title: Critical Diffusion Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Exponent boundaries separating qualitative diffusion behaviors.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_{\mathrm{dc}}=1-1/d\) and \(m_{\mathrm{mass}}=1-2/d\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes two critical exponents that govern different fast-diffusion properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal U_m(\rho)=(m-1)^{-1}\int\rho^m\,dx\), McCann displacement convexity holds when \(m\ge m_{\mathrm{dc}}=1-1/d\) and generally fails below this exponent. A distinct threshold \(m_{\mathrm{mass}}=(d-2)/d\) governs whole-space fast diffusion: above it, integrable solutions in the standard class conserve mass, while at or below it mass loss or finite-time extinction may occur. Since \(m_{\mathrm{mass}}<m_{\mathrm{dc}}\), mass conservation does not by itself imply displacement convexity of the generating energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fast diffusion has distinct thresholds for displacement convexity and mass conservation; confusing them obscures different failure mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical Diffusion Thresholds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two stated exponents concern distinct phenomena and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the mass-conservation, mass-loss, and extinction claims are sensitive to solution class and initial data. They require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Aggregation Flows
children.top_down_role: Continuum transport driven by collective concentration effects.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is even, attractive, and sufficiently regular for the continuity equation and convolution to be defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_t\) follows the attractive Wasserstein gradient flow of the interaction energy.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard interaction-energy formulation of attractive aggregation equations
source_gap: supplied locators do not support Wasserstein aggregation flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuum aggregation driven solely by an attractive pair potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\), define \(\mathcal E_W(\rho)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}W(x-y)\,d\rho(x)\,d\rho(y)\). An aggregation flow is a distributional solution of \[\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho_t v_t)=0,\qquad v_t=-\nabla(W*\rho_t),\qquad \rho_{t=0}=\rho_0.\] Whenever the first variation exists, \(\delta\mathcal E_W/\delta\rho=W*\rho\), so the displayed velocity is the negative Wasserstein gradient. Attraction means that this drift tends to decrease pairwise separation, subject to the chosen sign convention for \(W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An aggregation flow transports mass down the interaction energy generated by an attractive pair potential.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited, and the local inventory does not support aggregation equations in Wasserstein space. The mathematical formulation also leaves “attractive” and “sufficiently regular” undefined, while absolute continuity of the initial measure alone does not justify existence of the asserted distributional gradient flow. The plain statement omits these qualifications. The definition container is plausible, but a dedicated source and precise convention for attraction are required.

For \(W=W_{\mathrm a}+W_{\mathrm r}\), set \[\mathcal E(ho)= rac12\iint W_{\mathrm a}(x-y)\,dho(x)dho(y)+ rac12\iint W_{\mathrm r}(x-y)\,dho(x)dho(y).\] The attractive-repulsive flow is \[\partial_tho_t+

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tangency of \(v_t\) to \(K\) yields an evolution remaining in the admissible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Viability condition for a closed constraint set in Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuity-equation evolution \(\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho_t v_t)=0\) is constraint-preserving for \(K\) if \(\rho_0\in K\) and \(v_t\in T_K(\rho_t)\) for almost every \(t\). For an ambient driving velocity \(u_t\), the constrained steepest admissible velocity is formally \[v_t=P_{T_K(\rho_t)}u_t,\] whenever this metric projection is defined. Equivalently, \(u_t-v_t\in N_K(\rho_t)\) and \(v_t\in T_K(\rho_t)\). Under an applicable viability theorem, these conditions imply \(\rho_t\in K\) throughout the interval of existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Wasserstein flow preserves a closed constraint when its velocity remains tangent to the admissible set almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Preserving Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the constraint-preserving-flow container, but a generic closed subset of Wasserstein space need not have a convex tangent cone admitting the stated metric projection, nor does the displayed normal-cone relation follow without specifying compatible tangent and normal notions. children.title: Hard-Capacity Flow Regimes
children.top_down_role: Transport behavior near strict density ceilings.

assumptions_latex: \(K=\{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega):0\leq\rho\leq1\text{ a.e.}\}\) is nonempty and closed in the chosen Wasserstein topology.
\(\mathcal F\) is proper and lower semicontinuous on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizing-movement limit is a hard-capacity Wasserstein flow for \(\mathcal F+I_K\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard constrained JKO minimizing-movement scheme
source_gap: convergence hypotheses and topology require a dedicated source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete minimizing movement for an impenetrable upper density bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(\rho^0\in K\) and \(\tau>0\), define recursively \[\rho^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\rho\in K}\left\{\mathcal F(\rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\rho,\rho^k)\right\}.\] Equivalently, each step minimizes \(\mathcal F+I_K+W_2^2(\,
\cdot\,,\rho^k)/(2\tau)\), where \(I_K(\rho)=0\) for \(\rho\in K\) and \(I_K(\rho)=+\infty\) otherwise. The piecewise-constant interpolation is \(\rho_\tau(t)=\rho^k\) for \(t\in[k\tau,(k+1)\tau)\). Any convergent limit as \(\tau\downarrow0\) is the associated hard-capacity flow, subject to the hypotheses ensuring compactness and identification of the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard-capacity flow is obtained by JKO steps restricted to densities that never exceed the prescribed cap.
knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Capacity Flow Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed constrained JKO recursion is an algorithm, but the terminal title denotes hard-capacity flow regimes rather than specifically a numerical or minimizing-movement algorithm. More importantly, proper lower semicontinuity and closedness alone do not ensure existence of every minimizer, compactness, convergence, or identification of a gradient-flow limit. A dedicated source is needed to determine the necessary coercivity, topology, and limiting notion before either the algorithmic role or the conclusion can be accepted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For discrete measures \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\delta_{x_i}\) and \(
u=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\delta_{y_j}\), the transport problem is \[\min_{\pi\in\mathbb R_+^{m	imes n}}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}\pi_{ij}\quad	ext{subject to}\quad \sum_{j=1}^n\pi_{ij}=a_i,
\quad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=b_j.\] Every feasible \(\pi\) is a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(
u\), and every discrete coupling has this form. With \(c_{ij}=d(x_i,y_j)^p\), the optimum equals \(W_p^p(\mu,
u)\) whenever the ground metric and finite-moment assumptions defining \(W_p\) hold.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative enlargement of a feasible configuration set using configurations that violate the current full-dual inequality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal network simplex specialized to the balanced transport network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a feasible tree basis and its basic flow \(\pi\). At each iteration choose potentials satisfying \(u_i+v_j=c_{ij}\) on basic arcs and compute \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-u_i-v_j\) on nonbasic arcs. If every \(\bar c_{ij}\geq0\), output \(\pi\). Otherwise select an arc with \(\bar c_{ij}<0\), insert it into the tree, and augment flow around the unique resulting cycle in the cost-decreasing orientation until a subtracting arc reaches zero. Remove such an arc to restore a tree basis and repeat. A deterministic anti-cycling rule is required when a pivot is degenerate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square one-to-one minimum-cost assignment and its integral relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linear assignment problem is \[\min_{x\geq0}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1,
\quad \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1.\] Its feasible set is the set of doubly stochastic matrices. Its extreme points are permutation matrices, so the linear program has an optimal integral solution. Equivalently, its value is \[\min_{\sigma\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n c_{i,\sigma(i)}.\] Thus imposing \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) does not change the optimal value, although it restricts feasible points to assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The assignment LP minimizes total cost over doubly stochastic matrices and always has an optimal permutation-matrix solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Assignment Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The LP representation and permutation optimum fit the Linear Assignment Problems container and are standard for finite real costs. The integrality conclusion relies on the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem, but no inspectable citation is supplied. An authoritative locator supporting both the doubly stochastic formulation and extreme-point characterization is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-auction update for linear assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization, bidding update, reassignment operation, and stopping rule for the square linear-assignment auction algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize $S=\varnothing$, the partial assignment $\xi$ empty, and $\mathbf g=\mathbf0_n$. For $i\notin S$, choose
\[j_i^1\in\operatorname*{argmin}_j(C_{ij}-g_j),\qquad j_i^2\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{j\ne j_i^1}(C_{ij}-g_j),\]
and set
\[g_{j_i^1}^+=g_{j_i^1}-\big[(C_{i,j_i^2}-g_{j_i^2})-(C_{i,j_i^1}-g_{j_i^1})+\varepsilon\big].\]
If $i'\in S$ has $\xi_{i'}=j_i^1$, remove $i'$; then set $\xi_i^+=j_i^1$ and add $i$. Repeat until $S=\llbracket n\rrbracket$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from no assignments and a zero dual vector, an unassigned row bids for its best adjusted-cost column using the gap to its second-best column plus epsilon. Any previous owner is evicted, the bidding row is assigned, and the process stops when all rows are assigned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_{j_i^1}^+=g_{j_i^1}-\big[(C_{i,j_i^2}-g_{j_i^2})-(C_{i,j_i^1}-g_{j_i^1})+\varepsilon\big],\quad S^+=\bigl(S\setminus\{i'\in S:\xi_{i'}=j_i^1\}\bigr)\cup\{i\},\quad\xi_i^+=j_i^1

assumptions_latex: \(G=(U,V,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph with disjoint vertex classes \(U\) and \(V\).
\(w:E\to\mathbb R\) is specified when a weighted objective is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible incidence vectors are integral matchings, with perfection characterized by degree one at every vertex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard integral formulation of bipartite matching
source_gap: no supplied locator supports matching polytope claims
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bipartite matching, including weighted and perfect variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) such that no two edges of \(M\) share an endpoint. Its incidence vector satisfies \[x_e\in\{0,1\},\qquad \sum_{e\in\delta(z)}x_e\leq1\quad\text{for every }z\in U\cup V.\] A maximum-cardinality matching maximizes \(\sum_{e\in E}x_e\); a maximum-weight matching maximizes \(\sum_{e\in E}w(e)x_e\). A matching is perfect when equality holds in every vertex constraint. For bipartite graphs, relaxing \(x_e\in\{0,1\}\) to \(x_e\geq0\) leaves an integral matching polytope, so a linear objective admits an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite matching selects nonincident edges; weighted, cardinality, and perfect matching arise from different objectives or degree requirements.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Matching Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matching and perfect-matching clauses are definitions appropriate to the container, but the final relaxation-integrality assertion is a nontrivial theorem and should not be accepted as part of a generic definition without evidence. No citation supports the bipartite matching polytope claim. A source is required, and the record may need separation into a definition and an integrality property or theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete Bipartite Graph, Matching, and Perfect Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational graph definitions used for balanced assignment and bipartite-matching problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For n\in\mathbb{N}, the complete bipartite graph \mathcal{G}=K_{n,n} has vertex set \mathcal{V}=\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{R}, where \mathcal{L}=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}, \mathcal{R}=\{v'_1,\ldots,v'_n\}, and edge set \mathcal{E}=\{[v_i,v'_j]:v_i\in\mathcal{L},\ v'_j\in\mathcal{R}\}. A matching is a subset M\subseteq\mathcal{E} such that no two edges in M have a common endpoint. A matching is perfect if |M|=n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete balanced bipartite graph has two parts of n vertices and every edge joining the two parts. A matching has no two edges sharing an endpoint; in this graph it is perfect when it has n edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is a matching if no two edges of }M\text{ share an endpoint, and such a matching is perfect if }|M|=n.

children.title: Transport-to-Matching Reductions
children.top_down_role: Exact correspondences between transport instances and matching instances.

assumptions_latex: All discrete masses are rational multiples of a common unit \(1/N\).
The expanded bipartite graph assigns each copied pair the original transport cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum-cost perfect matching on the expanded graph has the same normalized value as the transport linear program.

notation.meaning: Number of matched copied pairs from type \(i\) to type \(j\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard replication reduction for rational discrete masses
source_gap: reduction and input-size implications need a computational transport source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact replication reduction for rational balanced masses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(a_i=A_i/N\) and \(b_j=B_j/N\), where \(A_i,B_j\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(\sum_iA_i=\sum_jB_j=N\). Replace source \(i\) by \(A_i\) copies and target \(j\) by \(B_j\) copies, and connect every source copy to every target copy with cost \(c_{ij}/N\). A perfect matching defines integers \(k_{ij}\) counting matched copy pairs and the transport plan \(\pi_{ij}=k_{ij}/N\). Conversely, every integral feasible table \(k\) with these margins can be realized by a perfect matching. Therefore the expanded matching optimum equals the rational transport optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational transport masses can be replicated into unit copies, turning balanced transport exactly into minimum-cost perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport-to-Matching Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The replication construction fits Transport-to-Matching Reductions and its cost normalization is internally consistent. However, the converse from a rational transport optimum to an integral table relies on transportation-polytope integrality, not merely on rational masses, and that dependence is not stated. The expanded instance can also be pseudo-polynomial in the encoded denominator N. A computational source is required to support the exact reduction and clarify its input-size implications.

children.title: Degenerate Transport Optima
children.top_down_role: Nonunique or combinatorially degenerate discrete solutions.

assumptions_latex: The balanced \(m\)-by-\(n\) transportation polytope is nonempty.
\(\pi\) is a basic feasible transport plan.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy occurs exactly when the basic plan has fewer than \(m+n-1\) positive entries.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard transportation-polytope characterization of primal degeneracy
source_gap: no supplied locator supports transport-basis degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal degeneracy of basic feasible solutions in balanced transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because one balance equation is redundant, a nondegenerate transportation basis has \(m+n-1\) basic variables. A basic feasible plan \(\pi\) is degenerate when at least one basic variable equals zero; equivalently, \[|\operatorname{supp}_+(\pi)|<m+n-1.\] The positive support graph \(G_+(\pi)\), with source and target vertices and edges where \(\pi_{ij}>0\), is then a forest that does not itself contain enough edges to form a spanning-tree basis. Zero-flow basic edges must be added to complete such a basis. An optimal plan is a degenerate transport optimum when it is both optimal and degenerate in this sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic transport optimum is degenerate when fewer than the expected number of basic arcs carry positive mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Transport Optima

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Degenerate Transport Optima, but the claimed equivalence with fewer than m+n-1 positive entries requires the standard full-rank transportation setting, typically positive row and column margins after zero-mass nodes are removed. Under the stated assumption of mere nonemptiness, the constraint rank can be smaller and the equivalence can fail. A source is needed to fix the basis convention and hypotheses before the definition can be accepted.

children.title: Sparse Transport Supports
children.top_down_role: Support sparsity in exact discrete couplings.

assumptions_latex: The transport cost is linear: \(\langle C,\pi\rangle\) over \(\Pi(a,b)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an optimal coupling \(\pi^\star\) satisfying \(|\operatorname{supp}(\pi^\star)|\le m+n-1\).

notation.meaning: Transportation polytope with prescribed row and column marginals.
Indices of strictly positive transport entries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite discrete balanced transport with linear cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear objective over the nonempty transportation polytope \(\Pi(a,b)\) attains its minimum at an extreme point. Consequently, for every cost matrix \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), some optimizer \(\pi^\star\in\arg\min_{\pi\in\Pi(a,b)}\langle C,\pi\rangle\) has at most \(m+n-1\) positive entries. Its support graph on the \(m+n\) row and column vertices is a forest; degeneracy may make the support strictly smaller than \(m+n-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite balanced discrete transport problem has an optimal coupling supported on at most m+n−1 pairs; degenerate optimal vertices may use fewer.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Transport Supports

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and content kind fit the leaf and are mathematically standard, but no source with a specific locator supports the extreme-point support bound or forest characterization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite two-marginal Kantorovich transport with compatible marginals.
